name: AI Engineer
role: Ships AI-powered products: prompts, tools, RAG, evals, APIs, hardening. Day to day: features, golden sets, traces, cost/latency. Differs from Architect (system shape) and Inference (engines): you own the application that calls the model.

subjects.title: LLM Application Fundamentals
subjects.why: Every product starts as messages, tokens, and a reliable client.
subjects.explainer:
Production LLM apps are distributed systems that speak chat APIs. Master streaming SSE, retries with jitter, deadlines, cancellation, and token accounting. Know the difference between chat, completions, and newer responses-style APIs. Structured JSON mode and schema adherence prevent brittle string parsing.

Message design (system/user/assistant/tool) and chat templates are part of the contract with the model. Context budgets are product decisions: what stays, what summarizes, what retrieves.

Common mistake: unbounded retries that amplify outages and bills. Another: blocking the request thread on a 60s model call with no timeout.

Wrap the vendor SDK behind your own client so you can swap providers and add telemetry once.

topics.title: Client Craft

subtopics.title: Chat vs completions vs responses APIs
subtopics.text: Chat APIs take a message list; older completions APIs take one text prompt; newer responses-style APIs add built-in tools and optional server-side conversation state.

subtopics.title: Idempotency and retries
subtopics.text: Make writes idempotent with a request ID so a retry doesn't create a duplicate order or email.

subtopics.title: Timeouts and cancellation
subtopics.text: Set a deadline per request and cancel the stream when the user leaves, so you stop paying for tokens nobody reads.

topics.explainer: A solid LLM client handles the boring failures. Know the API shapes: chat completions, newer responses-style APIs with built-in tools and state, and legacy completions. Streaming uses server-sent events; parse incrementally and handle disconnects. Retry 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff and jitter, and use idempotency keys when the call triggers side effects. Set connect and total timeouts and propagate user cancellation so you stop paying for tokens nobody will read. Log input, output and cached token counts on every call so cost is measurable per feature.

topics.title: Message Design

subtopics.title: Roles and chat templates
subtopics.text: The system message sets rules, user messages carry requests, assistant messages hold prior replies and tool messages return tool results.

subtopics.title: Context budgets
subtopics.text: Decide how many tokens each part of the prompt may use (instructions, examples, history, retrieved text) and keep room for the answer.

topics.explainer: Messages carry roles (system, user, assistant, tool) that the provider turns into a chat template. Put durable instructions in the system message and task data in user turns. Few-shot examples help most for format and edge cases; keep them short and representative. Budget context explicitly: instructions, retrieved data, history and room for the answer must fit. For multi-turn apps, decide what state you keep server-side versus resend each turn. Providers differ in tool-call formats, max output limits and how they treat system prompts, so wrap them in an adapter.

quiz.q: Streaming primarily improves…
quiz.why: Users see tokens sooner; quality unchanged.

quiz.q: Which errors should a client usually retry with backoff?
quiz.why: Rate limits and transient server errors are retryable; client errors are not.

quiz.q: Propagating user cancellation to the model call mainly saves…
choices: Tokens and money spent on output nobody reads
quiz.why: Generation keeps billing until the request stops.

lesson.intuition: Calling an LLM looks like one line of code, but in production it is a network call to a slow, sometimes overloaded, metered service that returns text a piece at a time. Application fundamentals are about treating it like any other unreliable dependency: stream results, set deadlines, retry safely, count tokens and keep the conversation state in your hands.
how: Build the request: a list of messages with roles (system, user, assistant, tool) plus settings such as model, max output tokens and response format.
Send it with a deadline and stream the response (server-sent events) so users see tokens immediately.
On rate limits (429) or server errors (5xx), retry with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a limit; never blindly retry side effects.
Record usage from the response (input, cached and output tokens) and convert to cost.
Store the conversation state yourself (or use a provider's stored-state API deliberately) and trim or summarize it to fit the context budget.
lesson.example: Exponential backoff with full jitter: base 0.5 s, cap 8 s. Attempt n waits a random time between 0 and min(8, 0.5 × 2ⁿ) seconds: up to 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 8 s. The worst-case total wait over 5 retries is 23 s, so a 30 s request deadline still has room for the final attempt.
mistakes: Retrying without jitter, so thousands of clients retry at the same moment and keep the provider overloaded.
Parsing free text with regexes instead of using structured output (JSON schema) modes.
Not setting max output tokens, so a runaway answer blows the latency and cost budget.
lesson.enterprise: A travel company's chatbot timed out during a provider incident because each request waited 60 s. Setting a 15 s deadline, streaming, and falling back to a second provider after two failed attempts kept 98% of conversations working during the next incident.
takeaways: Treat the model API as an unreliable, metered network dependency.
Stream, set deadlines, retry with jitter.
Count tokens on every call.
lesson.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant API as Model API
  App->>API: messages + settings (deadline 15s)
  API-->>App: 429 rate limited
  App->>App: backoff with jitter
  App->>API: retry
  API-->>App: stream tokens (SSE)
  API-->>App: usage: in / cached / out tokens
  App->>App: log cost, update state
lesson.diagramAlt: Sequence diagram: the app sends messages with a deadline, gets a rate-limit error, backs off with jitter, retries, receives streamed tokens and usage, then logs cost and updates state.

subjects.title: Prompt & Context Engineering
subjects.why: Most quality gains before fine-tuning live here.
subjects.explainer:
Prompting is specifying behavior under uncertainty. Clear instructions, constraints, schemas, and carefully chosen examples beat purple prose. Context engineering decides what enters the window: system policy, retrieved evidence, tool results, memory summaries — and in what order.

Lost-in-the-middle, recency bias, and compaction loss are practical failure modes. Prefer explicit refusal rules over hoping the model abstains.

Common mistake: a 4,000-word system prompt nobody diffs. Another: stuffing retrieval without citations or overlap checks.

Treat prompts as versioned code with evals on every change.

topics.title: Techniques

subtopics.title: CoT vs no-CoT
subtopics.text: Asking the model to reason step by step can help on multi-step problems; reasoning models already do this internally, so extra instructions may add only cost.

subtopics.title: Self-consistency
subtopics.text: Self-consistency samples several answers and takes the majority, which improves accuracy on reasoning tasks at several times the cost.

subtopics.title: Structured output / JSON schema
subtopics.text: Structured output modes constrain the model to a JSON schema so the result always parses.

topics.explainer: Clear prompts state the task, the audience, constraints and the output format, and include an example when format matters. Chain-of-thought helps on multi-step reasoning but costs tokens; reasoning models do it internally, so explicit CoT prompts matter less there. Self-consistency samples several answers and takes the majority, trading cost for accuracy. Use JSON schema or structured output modes instead of begging for JSON. Wrap untrusted content in clear delimiters and tell the model it is data, which helps but does not stop determined injection.

topics.title: Context Engineering

subtopics.title: Ordering and recency
subtopics.text: Models weigh recent and early content more. Put critical instructions at the start and repeat key constraints near the end of long prompts.

subtopics.title: Compaction / summarization
subtopics.text: When conversations get long, summarize older turns and drop stale tool output, but keep IDs, numbers and decisions verbatim.

topics.explainer: Context engineering means choosing what goes into the window and in what order. Sources include the system prompt, retrieved documents, memory, tool results and conversation history. Models attend best to the start and end, so put key instructions and the most relevant evidence there. When history grows, compact it by summarizing older turns while pinning facts that must survive. Require citations to retrieved chunks so answers can be verified. Most quality problems in production apps are context problems, not model problems.

quiz.q: Context engineering is mainly about…
choices: What enters the window and in what form
quiz.why: Selection and arrangement of context dominate quality.

quiz.q: Untrusted content in a prompt should be…
quiz.why: Clear boundaries help, though they do not fully stop injection.

quiz.q: Models tend to use information best when it is placed…
choices: At the start or end of the context
quiz.why: "Lost in the middle" degrades recall for centered content.

lesson.intuition: A prompt is a job description for a very capable new hire who knows nothing about your company and takes everything literally. Clear goals, rules, examples and the right reference material produce reliable work; vague instructions and a pile of irrelevant documents produce confident guesses. Context engineering is choosing what goes in front of the model, and in what order.
how: State the task, audience and output format explicitly, ideally with a schema.
Add constraints and refusal rules (for example 'If the answer is not in the sources, say so').
Add 2-5 diverse examples if format or tone matters.
Assemble context in a deliberate order: stable instructions first, then retrieved evidence with IDs, then the user's request.
Version the prompt and test every change against an eval set.
lesson.example: A before-and-after: 'Summarize this ticket' produced summaries of varying length that missed the customer's ask 30% of the time on a 50-ticket eval. The revised prompt specified 'Return JSON {issue, customer_ask, sentiment, next_step}; customer_ask must quote the customer if possible' with two examples. On the same 50 tickets, missing asks fell to 4% and every output parsed.
mistakes: A 4,000-word system prompt that nobody versions or diffs.
Stuffing every retrieved chunk into the prompt, burying the relevant one.
Changing several prompt parts at once without an eval, so you can't tell what helped.
lesson.enterprise: A bank's compliance assistant must cite policy sections. The prompt requires a citation ID for every claim and an explicit 'not found in policy' answer otherwise; an automated check rejects answers whose citations don't match retrieved chunk IDs.
takeaways: Be explicit about task, format and refusal rules.
Order context deliberately; less but relevant beats more.
Treat prompts as versioned, tested code.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SYS[Stable instructions + schema] --> CTX[Context assembly]
  EX[Examples] --> CTX
  RET[Retrieved evidence with IDs] --> CTX
  MEM[Memory summary] --> CTX
  USER[User request] --> CTX
  CTX --> LLM[Model]
  LLM --> VAL[Schema + citation check]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: stable instructions, examples, retrieved evidence, memory and the user request are assembled into context for the model, whose output is validated against schema and citations.

subjects.title: Tokenizer & Embedding Internals for App Devs
subjects.why: Token and embedding choices silently set cost and recall.
subjects.explainer:
You rarely train a tokenizer, but you must know fertility, multilingual blowups, and how embedding models differ from the chat model. Chunk boundaries that split sentences kill retrieval. Dimension, MRL, and similarity metrics affect index design.

Common mistake: embedding with model A and assuming chat model B 'understands' the same vectors. Another: giant chunks to 'save' embeddings that then exceed useful context.

Measure tokens per page of your real corpus before pricing the product.

topics.title: Tokenizers

subtopics.title: Fertility by domain
subtopics.text: Code, URLs, numbers and rare jargon often split into many tokens, so the same page can cost very different amounts.

subtopics.title: Truncation strategies
subtopics.text: When text is too long, decide what to cut: oldest turns, middle of documents, or low-ranked chunks. Never cut silently.

topics.explainer: Token counts drive cost, latency and truncation. Measure fertility on your real data: JSON, code, logs and non-English text often tokenize poorly. Special tokens such as end-of-turn markers must never appear in user content unescaped. When text is too long, choose a truncation strategy deliberately (keep the head and tail, summarize the middle, or retrieve) instead of chopping silently. Count tokens with the provider's tokenizer before sending so you can reject or compact oversized requests early.

topics.title: Embeddings

subtopics.title: Bi-encoders vs cross-encoders
subtopics.text: Bi-encoders embed query and document separately (fast, used for search); cross-encoders read them together (slower, more accurate, used for reranking).

subtopics.title: Dimension and MRL
subtopics.text: Matryoshka representation learning trains embeddings so the first N dimensions are still useful, letting you trade size for accuracy.

subtopics.title: Asymmetric query/doc models
subtopics.text: Some models use different prefixes or encoders for queries and documents; using the wrong one lowers recall.

topics.explainer: Embeddings turn text into vectors for search. Bi-encoders embed queries and documents separately, which is fast and indexable; cross-encoders read the pair together and are more accurate, so use them to rerank a shortlist. Matryoshka (MRL) models let you truncate vectors to fewer dimensions with modest quality loss, saving memory. Cosine similarity is standard; normalize vectors so dot product equals cosine. Some models use different prefixes or encoders for queries and documents. Re-evaluate when your domain drifts, and remember that changing embedding models means re-indexing.

topics.title: Context engineering and token economics
topics.explainer: Context engineering decides what goes into each call and in what order. Treat the window as a budget: reserve output tokens, then fixed costs (system prompt, tool schemas), then split the rest among retrieved evidence, conversation history and memory by priority. Put stable content first so prompt caching hits. When history overflows, compress older turns into summaries, drop stale tool outputs, and keep identifiers verbatim. Measure cost per task, not per call, because agents make many calls and input tokens dominate the bill.

subtopics.title: Context assembly order and prompt caching
subtopics.text: Stable content first (system prompt, tools) maximizes prompt-cache hits; variable content goes last.

subtopics.title: Context compression: summaries, pruning stale tool output
subtopics.text: Summarize old turns and drop stale tool outputs so the window holds what matters now.

subtopics.title: Cost per task vs cost per call

quiz.q: A bi-encoder is typically used to…
quiz.why: Bi-encoders enable fast retrieval.

quiz.q: Matryoshka (MRL) embeddings let you…
choices: Truncate vectors to fewer dimensions with modest quality loss
quiz.why: Prefixes of the vector remain useful embeddings.

quiz.q: After L2-normalizing vectors, dot product equals…
quiz.why: Normalization removes magnitude, leaving the cosine.

quiz.q: A 32k window reserves 4k for output and 5k for system and tools. Retrieval gets 60% of the rest. How many tokens is that?
Why put the stable system prompt and tool schemas first?
quiz.why: Caches match on identical prefixes, so stable content goes first.

lesson.intuition: Tokens are the unit you pay for and the unit that fills the context window, and embeddings are how text becomes searchable numbers. You rarely build either, but your choices about chunk size, which embedding model to use and how to budget the window quietly decide your costs and how well retrieval works.
how: Measure tokens on your real data, per language and document type, with the target model's tokenizer.
Pick an embedding model suited to your domain and languages; embed queries and documents with the same model (or its paired query/document versions).
Choose a similarity metric (usually cosine) and dimension; check whether the model supports shortening vectors (Matryoshka).
Allocate the context window by priority: output reserve, fixed instructions, then retrieval, history and memory.
Track cost per task, since agents make many calls.
lesson.example: Index sizing: 2 million chunks with 1,024-dimension float32 vectors need 2,000,000 × 1,024 × 4 bytes ≈ 8.2 GB for raw vectors. Truncating to 256 dimensions (if the model supports Matryoshka embeddings) gives ≈ 2.0 GB, and int8 quantization of 256 dimensions gives ≈ 0.5 GB, each at some recall cost you should measure.
mistakes: Embedding with one model and querying with another; the vector spaces don't match.
Using huge chunks to save embedding calls, which then dilute retrieval and fill the context.
Pricing a product from English samples when users write in other languages.
lesson.enterprise: A global support team measured tokens per ticket by language before launch. Thai and Hindi tickets used roughly twice the tokens of English for the same content with their chosen model, so they budgeted per language and picked a model with a more efficient tokenizer for those markets.
takeaways: Measure tokens on real data before pricing.
Same embedding model for queries and documents.
Budget the window; reserve output space.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  TXT[Document] --> CH[Chunker]
  CH --> EMB[Embedding model]
  EMB --> V[(Vectors: dim x bytes)]
  Q[Query] --> EMB
  V --> SIM[Cosine similarity]
  SIM --> TOP[Top-k chunks]
  TOP --> BUD[Context budget]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a document is chunked and embedded into vectors; queries use the same embedding model; cosine similarity picks top chunks that go into the context budget.

subjects.title: Tool Calling & Structured I/O
subjects.why: Tools turn chat into software; schemas keep it sane.
subjects.explainer:
Design task-oriented tools with strict schemas and server-side validation. Parallel tool calls, repair turns, max iterations, and human confirmation for irreversible side effects are part of the loop. Error messages back to the model should be actionable, not stack traces with secrets.

Common mistake: exposing 80 CRUD endpoints and wondering why tool selection flails. Another: trusting model-produced SQL without a permission layer.

Fewer, sharper tools beat a mirror of your REST API.

topics.title: Design

subtopics.title: Task-oriented vs CRUD
subtopics.text: Design tools around user tasks ('refund_order') rather than database tables ('update_row'), so the model needs fewer, safer steps.

subtopics.title: Descriptions models can use
subtopics.text: The description is the model's only documentation: say what the tool does, when to use it and what each argument means.

subtopics.title: Idempotent side effects
subtopics.text: Use idempotency keys so repeating a call (after a retry or a model loop) doesn't repeat the side effect.

topics.explainer: Design tools around tasks the model needs, not around your database tables: "refund_order(order_id, reason)" beats generic CRUD. Descriptions are prompts, so write them for the model, with when-to-use guidance and examples. Use strict argument schemas with enums and required fields. Classify side effects as read, reversible write or irreversible write, and make writes idempotent with keys so retries do not double-charge. Return compact, structured results and clear error messages the model can act on.

topics.title: Loop

subtopics.title: Error repair turns
subtopics.text: When a call fails, return a short message that says what was wrong and how to fix it, so the model can correct the arguments.

subtopics.title: Max iterations
subtopics.text: Set a hard cap on tool-call rounds so a confused agent can't loop forever.

topics.explainer: The tool loop is: model proposes calls, harness executes, results go back, repeat until the model answers. Run independent calls in parallel. When a tool fails, return a useful error so the model can repair arguments on the next turn rather than crashing. Cap iterations and total tokens so loops cannot run forever. Insert human confirmation before irreversible actions. Give each tool its own timeout so one slow API does not stall the whole run.

quiz.q: Tool results should be treated as…
choices: Untrusted input that can inject instructions
quiz.why: Tool outputs are an injection channel.

quiz.q: Idempotency keys on write tools prevent…
quiz.why: A retried call with the same key is a no-op.

quiz.q: When a tool fails, the harness should…
choices: Return a clear error so the model can repair its call
quiz.why: Actionable errors enable self-correction within budgets.

lesson.intuition: Tool calling lets a model ask your code to do things: look up an order, run a query, send an email. The model never runs the tool itself; it emits a structured request and your code decides whether and how to execute it. Good tools are like good APIs for a smart but literal colleague: few, clearly named, strictly typed and safe to retry.
how: Define a small set of task-oriented tools, each with a clear name, description and JSON schema for arguments.
The model returns a tool call with arguments; your code validates them against the schema and the user's permissions.
Execute the tool with a timeout; return a concise result or an actionable error message.
Feed results back to the model, which may call more tools (possibly in parallel) or answer.
Stop at a maximum number of iterations, and require human confirmation for irreversible actions.
lesson.example: Tool design: instead of exposing get_customer, get_orders, get_shipments and get_refunds (four calls and lots of IDs), expose one tool get_order_status(order_id) that returns {status, carrier, eta, refund_state}. On a 100-question eval of order queries, the agent's average tool calls fell from 3.4 to 1.1 and wrong answers from 12 to 3.
mistakes: Exposing dozens of CRUD endpoints so the model struggles to pick the right one.
Running model-generated SQL or shell commands without a permission layer or sandbox.
Returning raw stack traces (possibly with secrets) to the model as errors.
lesson.enterprise: A bank's assistant can look up balances and prepare transfers. The transfer tool only creates a draft that the customer approves in the app; the model can never move money directly, and all tool calls are logged with arguments.
takeaways: Fewer, sharper tools beat a mirror of your REST API.
Validate every call server-side; the model is not an authority.
Cap iterations and gate side effects.

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant M as Model
  participant H as Your code
  participant T as Tool
  U->>M: Where is order 123?
  M->>H: call get_order_status(order_id=123)

  H->>T: execute (timeout 5s)

  H-->>M: tool result
  M-->>U: Shipped, arriving Friday
lesson.diagramAlt: Sequence diagram: the user asks about an order, the model emits a tool call, your code validates and executes it with a timeout, returns the result, and the model answers.

subjects.title: RAG Systems Deep Dive
subjects.why: Retrieval is the default enterprise grounding path.
subjects.explainer:
Indexing (chunking, embeddings, metadata), hybrid BM25+dense, reranking, query rewrite, multi-hop, and citation grounding form the pipeline. Failures: wrong chunk, split fact, stale index, injection via docs, over-retrieval noise. GraphRAG and knowledge-graph hybrids help when relations matter more than similarity.

Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Refuse when unsupported.

Common mistake: one-size chunking for policies, tables, and code. Another: no ACL filters on the index in a multi-tenant app.

topics.title: Indexing

subtopics.title: Chunking strategies
subtopics.text: Chunk by structure where possible (headings, sections, table rows) rather than fixed character counts, and keep some overlap for context.

subtopics.title: Metadata and ACLs
subtopics.text: Store source, date, owner and access lists with each chunk so you can filter, cite and enforce permissions.

subtopics.title: Hybrid BM25+dense
subtopics.text: Keyword search catches exact identifiers; vector search catches paraphrases. Combining them is more robust than either.

topics.explainer: Indexing quality sets the ceiling for RAG. Chunk on structure (headings, sections) rather than fixed character counts, with modest overlap. Pick embeddings by testing retrieval on your data. Attach metadata (source, date, ACL, section) to every chunk so you can filter and cite. Combine BM25 keyword search with dense vectors, since each catches what the other misses. For complex corpora, hierarchical or graph indexes capture relationships that flat chunks lose.

topics.title: Query Path

subtopics.title: Reranking
subtopics.text: A cross-encoder reranker reads the question with each candidate chunk and reorders them, usually improving the top few a lot.

subtopics.title: Refusal and coverage
subtopics.text: If the evidence doesn't support an answer, the system should say so instead of guessing.

topics.explainer: At query time, rewrite vague or conversational questions into standalone searches; HyDE generates a hypothetical answer and searches with it. Multi-hop questions need iterative retrieval where each step informs the next. Retrieve broadly (say 50 candidates) then rerank with a cross-encoder down to the best 5 to 10. Force the model to cite chunk ids and to say when the evidence does not cover the question. Good refusals are a feature, not a failure.

topics.title: Failure Modes

subtopics.title: Wrong chunk / split fact
subtopics.text: A fact split across two chunks may never be retrieved together. Overlap, larger sections or parent-document retrieval help.

subtopics.title: Doc-based injection
subtopics.text: Retrieved documents can contain instructions. Treat them as data and never let them change tool permissions.

topics.explainer: RAG fails in recognizable ways. The answer was split across two chunks and neither alone is enough. The index is stale. A document contains injected instructions that the model follows. Too many weak chunks drown the relevant one. Evals only test easy questions so problems stay hidden. Diagnose by logging retrieved chunks with every answer and labeling failures as retrieval misses versus generation errors; the fixes are completely different.

topics.title: Knowledge graphs for RAG
topics.explainer: Knowledge graphs store entities and typed relationships, such as customer owns contract and contract references a policy, which supports multi-hop questions that chunk similarity misses. Build them by extracting entities and relations with an LLM, resolving duplicates, and storing them in a graph database. At query time, combine vector search to find entry points with graph traversal or Cypher queries to follow relations. GraphRAG adds community summaries for global questions. Graphs cost effort to maintain, so use them where relationships drive answers.

subtopics.title: Entities and relations
subtopics.text: A knowledge graph stores entities (people, products, contracts) as nodes and their relationships as edges.

subtopics.title: Vector entry points plus traversal
subtopics.text: Use vector search to find starting entities, then follow graph relations to collect connected facts for multi-hop questions.

subtopics.title: When knowledge graphs pay off
subtopics.text: Graphs pay off for multi-hop questions about relationships; for plain lookup questions, vector search is usually enough.

topics.title: Agentic RAG: query rewriting, self-correction and abstention
topics.explainer: Agentic RAG puts the model in control of retrieval. Rewrite the query first: expand acronyms, split multi-part questions, or generate a hypothetical answer to embed (HyDE). Use hybrid search (BM25 plus vectors) and contextual retrieval, which prepends a short chunk-specific context before embedding. Then grade the retrieved chunks. Corrective RAG (CRAG) rewrites and re-searches or falls back to web search when the grades are low, and Self-RAG trains the model to critique its own retrieval and support. If evidence stays weak after a capped number of retries, abstain and say what is missing.

subtopics.title: Query rewriting, decomposition and HyDE
subtopics.text: Rewrite vague queries, split complex ones into sub-questions, or embed a hypothetical answer (HyDE) to retrieve better.

subtopics.title: Relevance grading of retrieved chunks
subtopics.text: A grader (often a small LLM call) labels each retrieved chunk relevant or not, so the system knows when to retry or abstain.

subtopics.title: Abstention with retry caps
subtopics.text: If retrieval still finds nothing after a capped number of retries, say so instead of guessing.

quiz.q: Hybrid search combines…
quiz.why: Lexical+dense covers complementary failures.

quiz.q: Reranking with a cross-encoder is typically applied to…
quiz.why: Cross-encoders are accurate but too slow for full-corpus search.

quiz.q: To diagnose a bad RAG answer first check…
quiz.why: Separate retrieval misses from generation errors.

quiz.q: First-pass retrieval is relevant 70% of the time, and one rewrite fixes half of the failures. What is the success rate after one retry?
What should an agentic RAG system do when evidence is still weak after its retry cap?
choices: Abstain and state what is missing
quiz.why: Bounded retries followed by abstention prevent unsupported answers.

lesson.intuition: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is an open-book exam for the model. Instead of hoping it memorized your company's policies, you find the relevant pages and put them in front of it, then ask it to answer only from those pages and cite them. Most enterprise AI assistants are RAG systems, and most of their failures are retrieval failures.
how: Index: split documents into chunks with metadata (source, date, permissions), embed them and also build a keyword (BM25) index.
Query: optionally rewrite the question, then run hybrid search (vector + keyword) with permission filters.
Rerank the top candidates with a cross-encoder and keep the best few.
Generate: give the model the chunks with IDs and instruct it to answer only from them, citing IDs, or to say it doesn't know.
Evaluate retrieval (recall@k) and generation (faithfulness, correctness) separately.
lesson.example: Reciprocal rank fusion of keyword and vector results with k = 60: a chunk ranked 1st by BM25 and 3rd by vectors scores 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.0164 + 0.0159 = 0.0323. A chunk ranked 2nd by vectors only scores 1/62 ≈ 0.0161. The first chunk wins because both retrievers agree on it.
mistakes: Using one chunking strategy for policies, tables and code alike.
No permission filters, so users can retrieve documents they shouldn't see.
Only measuring final answers, so you can't tell whether retrieval or generation failed.
lesson.enterprise: An IT help desk assistant answers from 40,000 knowledge-base articles. Adding BM25 to vector search fixed failures on error codes like '0x80070005', and per-article permission filters keep HR-only articles out of general answers.
takeaways: RAG = retrieve, then answer from evidence with citations.
Hybrid search plus reranking is the strong default.
Measure retrieval and generation separately.

flowchart LR
  DOC[Documents] --> CH[Chunk + metadata + ACL]
  CH --> VI[(Vector index)]
  CH --> KI[(BM25 index)]
  Q[Question] --> RW[Rewrite]
  RW --> VI
  RW --> KI
  VI --> F[Fuse + rerank]
  KI --> F
  F --> G[Generate with citations]
  G --> A[Answer or 'not found']

subjects.title: Semantic Caching & Gateway Clients
subjects.why: Repeat traffic should not always pay full token price.
subjects.explainer:
Application-level semantic caches and gateway features (LiteLLM and friends) reduce spend on FAQs and repeated agent prefixes. Keys must include tenant, tool policy version, and model identity. Bypass on freshness-critical or personalized paths.

Common mistake: caching answers that include time-varying inventory. Another: sharing cache across permission tiers.

Instrument hit rate next to quality — a high hit rate with wrong answers is a silent outage.

topics.title: Design

subtopics.title: Similarity thresholds
subtopics.text: The similarity threshold trades hit rate against wrong answers. Tune it on labeled pairs of questions that should and shouldn't match.

subtopics.title: Key composition
subtopics.text: Include everything that changes the right answer: tenant, user role, model, prompt version and policy version.

subtopics.title: Bypass rules
subtopics.text: Skip the cache for requests that are personalized, depend on real-time data or trigger tools.

topics.explainer: Semantic caching stores responses keyed by prompt embeddings and returns a hit when a new prompt is similar enough. The similarity threshold is the main knob: too low and users get wrong answers, too high and nothing hits. Build keys from the embedding plus tenant, model, prompt version and relevant parameters. Use TTLs and event-based invalidation when source data changes. Bypass the cache for personalized or tool-using requests. Expect a cold start with no hits until traffic builds the cache.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Poisoned cache incidents
subtopics.text: If a wrong answer gets cached, every similar question gets it. Have a way to purge entries quickly.

subtopics.title: Versioned policy in keys
subtopics.text: Put the policy or prompt version in the key so changes automatically stop serving old answers.

topics.explainer: Track hit rate, false-hit rate (sampled and reviewed), latency saved and dollars saved. A poisoned cache, where one bad answer gets served thousands of times, is the classic incident, so keep a way to purge by key pattern instantly. Put the policy version in the key so changes invalidate old entries automatically. In multi-region deployments decide whether caches are regional or replicated. Attribute savings to teams so the value is visible.

quiz.q: Cache keys should change when…
choices: Model, prompt version, or permission scope changes
Only the wall clock changes by 1s
quiz.why: Semantic identity includes policy and model.

quiz.q: The classic semantic-cache incident is…
choices: One wrong answer served thousands of times
quiz.why: Keep the ability to purge entries instantly.

quiz.q: Personalized or tool-using requests should usually…
quiz.why: Their correct answers depend on user-specific state.

lesson.intuition: Many requests repeat: the same FAQ, the same long system prompt, the same document asked about twice. Caching avoids paying full price every time. Exact caches reuse identical requests, prompt (prefix) caching reuses the provider's work on a repeated beginning of the prompt, and semantic caches reuse answers for questions that mean the same thing.
how: Use provider prompt caching first: keep the stable prefix identical across calls.
Add an exact-match cache for deterministic, repeated requests.
Add a semantic cache: embed the question and reuse a stored answer above a tuned similarity threshold.
Compose keys with tenant, model, prompt version and tool-policy version; set TTLs.
Bypass for personalized, time-sensitive or tool-using requests, and monitor hit rate next to quality.
lesson.example: Threshold tuning: on 1,000 labeled question pairs, a similarity threshold of 0.90 gives a 35% hit rate but 6% of hits return a wrong answer; 0.95 gives 22% hits with 0.5% wrong. If a wrong answer costs far more than an API call, 0.95 is the better choice even though it saves less.
mistakes: Caching answers that depend on live data such as stock levels.
Sharing a cache across permission tiers or tenants.
Celebrating a high hit rate without checking whether cached answers are correct.
lesson.enterprise: An e-commerce company caches answers to shipping and returns FAQs per country and per policy version. When the returns policy changes, bumping the policy version in the key invalidates all affected entries instantly.
takeaways: Prefix caching is the free win: order prompts stable-first.
Semantic cache thresholds need an eval.
Version and tenant belong in the key.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q[Request] --> K[Key: tenant + model + prompt v + policy v]
  K --> EX{Exact hit?}
  EX -->|yes| R[Return]
  EX -->|no| SEM{Semantic hit >= threshold?}
  SEM -->|yes| R
  SEM -->|no| LLM[Call model with cached prefix]
  LLM --> STORE[Store with TTL]
  STORE --> R
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a request builds a key with tenant and versions, checks an exact cache, then a semantic cache, and otherwise calls the model and stores the answer with a TTL.

subjects.title: Product Evals & Quality Loops
subjects.why: Ship with a gate, not a vibe check.
subjects.explainer:
Suites need capability, safety, and style slices; golden plus adversarial cases; process metrics for tools; cost and latency budgets. Put evals in CI. Calibrate judges. Sample production for new failures.

Common mistake: only happy-path demos in the suite. Another: changing model and prompt simultaneously without a factorial eval.

Make failing evals block merges for critical paths.

topics.title: Suite Design

subtopics.title: Golden + adversarial
subtopics.text: Golden cases are representative and labeled; adversarial cases try to break the system with tricky inputs or attacks.

subtopics.title: Process metrics
subtopics.text: For agents, check steps too: right tool, valid arguments, no unnecessary calls.

topics.explainer: A product eval suite covers capability (does it solve tasks), safety (refusals, leaks, harmful content) and style (tone, format). Mix golden examples from real traffic with adversarial cases. For agents, add process metrics such as steps taken and tool errors. Track cost and latency per case alongside quality so trade-offs are explicit. Slice results by user cohort, language and task type, because averages hide the segment that is failing.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Judge calibration
subtopics.text: Measure how often the LLM judge agrees with human labels and adjust the rubric until agreement is acceptable.

subtopics.title: Flaky eval hygiene
subtopics.text: Fix the seed, freeze test data and pin model versions so the same code gives the same score.

topics.explainer: Treat evals as code. Version prompts, models and judge configs together so results are reproducible. Calibrate LLM judges against human labels periodically. Sample production traffic into review queues to find new failure types and feed them back into the golden set. Show regression dashboards per release. Quarantine flaky cases and fix their nondeterminism rather than ignoring red results. Try it: run the same eval twice with no changes. Any case that flips is flaky and needs fixing before it can gate a release.

quiz.q: Process metrics for agents include…
choices: Whether the correct tool and args were chosen
quiz.why: Trajectory correctness matters.

quiz.q: Why slice eval results by cohort?
quiz.why: A 90% average can hide a 50% language or task slice.

quiz.q: A case that flips pass/fail with no changes is…
choices: Flaky and should be fixed before gating releases
quiz.why: Flaky cases erode trust in the eval gate.

lesson.intuition: Product evals are the test suite for an AI feature. They answer 'is this change better or worse?' with numbers instead of opinions. A good suite mixes everyday cases, hard cases and attacks, checks both answers and process (did it call the right tool?), and runs automatically on every change, blocking merges that make things worse.
how: Write slices: capability (does it do the task), safety (does it refuse what it should), style (tone, format).
Collect cases from real usage, add adversarial ones, and label expected outcomes or rubrics.
Grade with code where possible, with calibrated LLM judges elsewhere, and with humans for a sample.
Run in CI with baselines; fail the build on meaningful regressions in critical slices.
Sample production traffic, label failures and add them to the suite.
lesson.example: Factorial testing: changing model (A→B) and prompt (v1→v2) together raised accuracy from 81% to 86%. Running all four combinations on the same 400 cases showed A+v2 = 85%, B+v1 = 80%, B+v2 = 86%. Almost all of the gain came from the prompt; model B cost twice as much for 1 extra point.
mistakes: Only happy-path demo cases in the suite.
Changing model and prompt at once and crediting the wrong one.
Flaky evals (random seeds, live data) that teams learn to ignore.
lesson.enterprise: A legal-tech company's contract-review assistant has 600 eval cases sliced by clause type. A new prompt improved indemnity clauses but broke termination clauses; the CI gate on per-slice accuracy blocked the merge.
takeaways: Evals are the spec and the safety net.
Slice results; aggregates hide regressions.
Block merges on critical regressions.

subjects.title: Vector Search Internals
subjects.why: Retrieval quality and cost depend on how the index actually finds neighbors.
subjects.explainer:
Vector databases use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes such as HNSW, IVF and product quantization. Understanding their knobs lets you trade recall, latency and memory deliberately, size infrastructure, and avoid pitfalls such as filters that destroy recall.

Common mistakes: never measuring recall against exact search; post-filtering ANN results by tenant; re-embedding without re-indexing; choosing a vector DB before knowing data size and filter needs.

resources.why: The primary research paper behind this idea. Read the abstract, figures and method section to see where the technique comes from and what was actually measured.

subjects.project: Index 1M vectors with HNSW and IVF-PQ in Faiss. Plot recall@10 vs latency for several efSearch and nprobe values, measure memory, then add a tenant filter and observe recall with pre- vs post-filtering.

topics.title: ANN Algorithms
topics.explainer: Exact search is linear in corpus size. HNSW navigates a layered proximity graph and offers excellent recall and latency at the cost of memory (vectors plus links). IVF partitions vectors into clusters and searches only the closest nprobe lists, which is cheaper in memory and easy to shard. Product quantization compresses vectors into compact codes, enabling billions of vectors in RAM, usually with a full-precision rerank of top candidates. DiskANN-style indexes keep most data on SSD.

subtopics.title: HNSW graphs (M, ef)
subtopics.text: Higher M improves recall but uses more memory; higher ef (search) improves recall but slows queries.

subtopics.title: IVF lists and nprobe
subtopics.text: IVF assigns vectors to clusters; scanning more clusters (nprobe) raises recall and latency.

subtopics.title: Product quantization
subtopics.text: PQ splits each vector into sub-vectors and stores a small code for each, compressing memory by 10-50× with some loss.

topics.title: Operating Vector Indexes
topics.explainer: Measure recall@k against exact search on a sample whenever you change parameters or data. Size memory as vectors plus index overhead. Filters by tenant or ACL should be applied during search (filtered HNSW, partitioned indexes) rather than after, or results can come back nearly empty. Plan re-indexing when embedding models change and handle deletes, which some graph indexes support poorly. Hybrid keyword plus vector search is often the best default.

subtopics.title: Recall measurement
subtopics.text: Run the same queries with exact search and ANN, and count how many of the true top-k ANN found.

subtopics.title: Filtered search strategies
subtopics.text: Use pre-filtering or filter-aware indexes (or separate indexes per tenant) so restrictive filters don't destroy recall.

quiz.q: Increasing HNSW efSearch generally…
quiz.why: A wider search explores more candidates.

quiz.q: Product quantization mainly reduces…
quiz.why: Vectors become compact codes.

quiz.q: Post-filtering ANN results by tenant can cause…
choices: Few or no results when the tenant is small
quiz.why: Most top candidates may belong to other tenants.

quiz.q: 10M float32 vectors of 768 dims take about…

lesson.intuition: Finding the nearest vectors among millions by checking every one is slow. Vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes that check only a smart subset, like using a map of neighborhoods instead of knocking on every door. You trade a little recall for a lot of speed, and the index's knobs let you choose where on that trade-off you sit.
how: Exact search compares the query with every vector: perfect recall, cost grows linearly with data.
HNSW builds a multi-layer graph; search hops from coarse to fine layers toward nearer neighbors. M sets links per node, ef sets how many candidates to explore.
IVF clusters vectors; search only scans the nprobe nearest clusters.
Product quantization compresses vectors into short codes to save memory, at some accuracy cost.
Measure recall@k against exact search on a sample and tune the knobs to meet your latency and recall targets.
lesson.example: HNSW memory: 10M vectors × 768 dims × 4 bytes = 30.7 GB for vectors. With M = 16, the base layer stores about 2M = 32 neighbor links per node at 4 bytes each ≈ 128 bytes per vector, ≈ 1.3 GB more. Raising efSearch from 40 to 200 might lift recall@10 from 0.92 to 0.99 while roughly tripling query latency; measure on your data.
mistakes: Never measuring recall against exact search.
Filtering by tenant after ANN search, so few or no results survive the filter.
Re-embedding documents with a new model without rebuilding the index.
lesson.enterprise: A marketplace with 50M listings uses IVF-PQ to fit the index in memory on a few machines, and keeps an HNSW index for the 2M most active listings. Weekly recall checks against exact search on 1,000 sample queries catch degradation after data changes.
takeaways: ANN trades recall for speed; measure both.
Filters must be built into search, not applied afterward.
Size memory before choosing a database.

flowchart TB
  Q[Query vector] --> L2[Top layer: few nodes]
  L2 --> L1[Middle layer]
  L1 --> L0[Base layer: all nodes]
  L0 --> C[Candidate list size ef]
  C --> K[Top-k results]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: an HNSW search starts at a sparse top layer, descends through a middle layer to the base layer containing all nodes, keeps a candidate list of size ef and returns the top-k results.

subjects.title: Reasoning Models, Test-Time Compute and Model API Platform Features
subjects.why: Reasoning models and platform features (stateful APIs, caching, batch, built-in tools) change the cost and quality math of every agent.
subjects.explainer:
Reasoning models (OpenAI o-series and GPT reasoning modes, Claude with extended thinking, Gemini thinking, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen reasoning) spend extra tokens thinking before answering. This test-time compute boosts math, coding, planning and multi-step tool use, controlled by settings such as reasoning effort or a thinking budget. The trade-off is latency and cost: thinking tokens are billed, and simple tasks gain nothing.

Model APIs now bundle platform features that agents should use deliberately: the OpenAI Responses API with stored conversation state and built-in tools (web search, file search, code interpreter, computer use); prompt caching across OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini; batch APIs at roughly half price for offline jobs; structured outputs; citations; moderation endpoints; and fine-tuning including reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) with graders. Cloud platforms mirror these: Bedrock batch inference, model evaluation and Guardrails; Azure AI Foundry evaluations and content safety.

Common mistakes: max reasoning effort everywhere; dropping prior reasoning items between tool calls so the model re-thinks; online calls for work that could be batched; no caching on long stable system prompts.

Mental model: reasoning effort is a dial on cost per correct answer. Measure it.

topics.title: Reasoning models and test-time compute
topics.explainer: Reasoning models are trained, typically with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, to produce long internal chains of thought before answering. More thinking tokens generally improve accuracy on hard problems, with diminishing returns. APIs expose this as reasoning effort levels or thinking token budgets. For agents, reasoning helps planning and tool selection; keep reasoning state across tool calls where the API supports it (for example, passing back reasoning items or thinking blocks) to avoid repeated thinking. Route easy requests to non-reasoning models.

subtopics.text: Reasoning models are typically trained with reinforcement learning on tasks with checkable answers, which rewards useful step-by-step reasoning.

subtopics.title: Routing easy vs hard requests

topics.explainer: The Responses API can store conversation state server-side and run built-in tools such as web search, file search over uploaded files, code interpreter and computer use, which removes boilerplate but couples you to a vendor. Prompt caching discounts repeated prefixes, so put stable instructions and tool definitions first. Batch APIs process large offline jobs asynchronously at about half price within a 24-hour window; Bedrock batch inference is the cloud equivalent. Use streaming for user-facing latency and batch for everything that can wait.

Managed evaluation services (Bedrock model evaluation, Azure AI Foundry evaluations, OpenAI Evals) run LLM-as-judge and human evaluation jobs. Moderation and content safety APIs (OpenAI Moderation, Azure AI Content Safety with Prompt Shields, Bedrock Guardrails) classify harmful content and injection attempts. Use them as building blocks, while keeping your own golden sets as the source of truth.

quiz.q: A model at high reasoning effort is 2% more accurate but 4x the cost on simple FAQ questions. Best action?
choices: Route simple questions to low effort or a non-reasoning model
quiz.why: Optimize cost per correct answer by routing by difficulty.

quiz.q: Where should stable instructions and tool definitions go to benefit from prompt caching?
choices: At the start, as a stable prefix
At the end of the prompt
quiz.why: Caches match on identical prefixes.

quiz.q: Which workload fits a batch API?
quiz.why: Batch suits large, latency-tolerant offline jobs at lower price.

lesson.intuition: Reasoning models think before they answer: they generate hidden or summarized chains of reasoning, spending extra tokens (test-time compute) to solve harder problems. That makes them much better at math, code and planning, but slower and more expensive. Meanwhile model APIs now include built-in tools, caching and batch modes that change the cost and design of agents.
how: Decide which requests need reasoning (multi-step math, code, planning) and which don't (classification, simple lookups).
Set reasoning effort or a thinking budget; higher budgets help hard tasks but add latency and billed tokens.
When using tools with reasoning models, pass reasoning state back as the provider requires so the model keeps its train of thought.
Use platform features deliberately: prompt caching for repeated prefixes, batch APIs for offline jobs, built-in search or code tools when they fit.
Evaluate cost per correct answer for each setting and route easy requests to cheaper modes.
lesson.example: Thinking budget math: a task with 1,500 input tokens and a 300-token answer. With a reasoning model at $2 per 1M input and $8 per 1M output (thinking tokens are billed as output), low effort uses 1,000 thinking tokens: cost = 1,500×2/1M + 1,300×8/1M = $0.003 + $0.0104 = $0.0134. High effort uses 8,000 thinking tokens: $0.003 + 8,300×8/1M = $0.0694, about 5× more. Use high effort only where it measurably helps.
mistakes: Using maximum reasoning effort for every request.
Dropping the reasoning items between tool-use turns, which degrades multi-step performance.
Using realtime APIs for overnight jobs that could run at batch pricing.
lesson.enterprise: A financial analytics team routes spreadsheet-formula questions to low reasoning effort and multi-step forecasting questions to high effort. Monthly cost fell 60% versus 'always high', with no drop on their 300-question eval.
takeaways: Reasoning helps hard multi-step tasks; it wastes money on easy ones.
Thinking tokens are billed; budget them.
Use caching and batch features on purpose.

  C -->|no| FAST[Standard model / low effort]
  C -->|yes| THINK[Reasoning model, high effort]
  THINK --> TOOLS[Tools with preserved reasoning]

lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: requests are routed by difficulty to a standard model or a reasoning model with high effort and tools; offline jobs go to a batch API.

Start with workflows and state machines. Promote to a single tool-using agent when branching is truly model-driven. Use plan-act-observe loops with budgets. Subagents need clear contracts. Deterministic wrappers around brittle steps reduce variance.

Common mistake: a swarm for a form-fill. Another: no stop condition beyond 'model says done.'

Compare agent versus workflow on evals and cost before celebrating autonomy.

topics.title: When to Agent

subtopics.title: Workflow vs agent tree
subtopics.text: Draw the decision tree. If every branch is known, code it; use the model only for the branches that need judgment.

subtopics.title: State machines first
subtopics.text: A state machine with model-powered steps is easier to test and debug than a free agent.

subtopics.title: Budgeting
subtopics.text: Set caps on steps, tokens, wall-clock time and dollars per task.

topics.explainer: Most problems that look like agent problems are workflows: a fixed sequence of steps with an LLM inside some of them. Workflows are cheaper, faster and easier to test. Model the task as a state machine first. Use a single tool-using agent when steps genuinely depend on intermediate results. Only reach for multiple agents when tasks are parallel or need very different contexts. Always define human escalation and step, token and dollar budgets.

subtopics.title: Plan-Act-Observe
subtopics.text: Each turn the model plans an action, the harness executes it and appends the observation to the context.

subtopics.title: Subagents
subtopics.text: Sub-agents get a narrow task and return a compact result, keeping the main agent's context small.

topics.explainer: A practical agent runs plan, act, observe in a loop. A scratchpad or todo list keeps the plan visible across turns. Subagents can handle isolated subtasks with fresh context and return summaries. Wrap fragile operations in deterministic code rather than asking the model to do them. Make every side-effecting tool idempotent so a retry after a crash does not repeat work. Log the full trajectory for debugging and evals.

quiz.q: Prefer a workflow when…
choices: Every step needs creative tool choice
quiz.why: Deterministic pipelines beat agents when known.

quiz.q: Before building multiple agents you should…
choices: Try a workflow, then a single tool-using agent
quiz.why: Complexity should be earned by evidence.

quiz.q: A visible todo list or scratchpad in an agent helps…
choices: Keep the plan coherent across many turns
quiz.why: Explicit plans reduce drift.

lesson.intuition: An agent is a loop: the model looks at the goal and what has happened so far, decides the next action, a tool runs it, and the result comes back. That flexibility is great when the next step truly depends on what was just learned, and wasteful when the steps are known in advance. Good engineers start with a simple workflow and add autonomy only where it pays.
how: Map the task. If the steps are fixed, build a workflow or state machine; if they depend on results, consider an agent.
Start with one agent with a few good tools before adding sub-agents.
Run a plan-act-observe loop with a budget: maximum steps, tokens, time and cost.
Wrap brittle steps (parsing, API calls) in deterministic code, and make side effects idempotent.
Escalate to a human when confidence is low or the budget runs out, and evaluate agent vs workflow on the same tasks.
lesson.example: Agent vs workflow: on 200 expense-report tasks, a fixed 3-step workflow scored 91% at $0.012 per task. A free agent scored 93% at $0.045 with 4% runaway loops. A hybrid (workflow with an agent only for the 'unusual receipt' branch, 15% of tasks) scored 93% at ≈ $0.017. The hybrid kept the quality gain at a fraction of the cost.
mistakes: Building a multi-agent swarm for what is really a form fill.
Stopping only when 'the model says done', with no step or cost limit.
Not comparing the agent with a simpler workflow on the same eval.
lesson.enterprise: An IT operations team uses a workflow for password resets (fixed steps) and an agent for 'my laptop is slow' tickets, where diagnosis depends on what each check finds. The agent can run read-only diagnostics freely but needs approval to change settings.
takeaways: Workflow when steps are known; agent when they aren't.
Every loop needs a budget and a stop rule.
Measure agents against simpler baselines.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  G[Goal + state] --> P[Plan next step]
  P --> A[Act: tool call]
  A --> O[Observe result]
  O --> D{Done or budget hit?}
  D -->|no| P
  D -->|done| OUT[Answer]
  D -->|budget / low confidence| H[Escalate to human]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: an agent loop of plan, act and observe repeats until done, or escalates to a human when the budget runs out or confidence is low.

subjects.title: Production Hardening
subjects.why: Demos are not products.
subjects.explainer:
Timeouts, circuit breakers, fallback models, queues, backpressure, and idempotent writes keep systems alive. Observability needs structured traces of prompts, tools, tokens, and dollars — with PII redaction. AuthN/Z on tools, output filters, dependency pinning, and spend caps are mandatory.

Common mistake: logging raw prompts to a multi-tenant sink. Another: no kill switch when a prompt change loops tools.

On-call for AI includes quality pages, not only 5xx.

topics.title: Reliability

subtopics.title: Timeouts / breakers
subtopics.text: A timeout stops waiting; a circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency for a while so it can recover.

subtopics.title: Queues and backpressure
subtopics.text: Queues absorb bursts; backpressure tells callers to slow down instead of letting work pile up until memory runs out.

topics.explainer: Production LLM features need the reliability patterns of any distributed system. Set timeouts and circuit breakers on model calls. Configure fallback models or providers. Put async work on queues with backpressure so spikes do not cascade. Make writes idempotent. Shed low-priority load when capacity is short. Test these paths deliberately, because a provider outage is a matter of when, not if.

topics.title: Observability

subtopics.title: Structured traces
subtopics.text: Record a trace per request with spans for model calls and tools, including model, prompt version, tokens and latency.

subtopics.title: Token and $ metrics
subtopics.text: Track tokens and dollars per request, user and feature so cost spikes are visible.

subtopics.title: Redacted logs
subtopics.text: Strip personal and secret data from logs before storing them.

topics.explainer: Trace every request across retrieval, model calls and tools with structured spans (OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions help). Record tokens, cost, latency and model version per span. Sample outputs for quality review. Alert on drift in quality scores, refusal rates or tokens per request, not only on errors. Redact secrets and personal data before traces are stored, since traces are a common source of leaks.

topics.title: App Security

subtopics.title: AuthN/Z on tools
subtopics.text: Every tool call should check who the user is and whether they may perform that action.

subtopics.title: PII redaction
subtopics.text: Detect and mask personal data in inputs, outputs and logs.

subtopics.title: Spend caps
subtopics.text: Hard caps on spend per user, tenant and feature stop runaway loops and abuse.

topics.explainer: Authorize every tool call against the end user's permissions, not the app's service account. Filter outputs for sensitive data and unsafe content before display or action. Redact PII before sending to third-party models where possible. Pin dependency and model versions to avoid supply-chain surprises. Enforce spend caps per user and per key so an abuser or a runaway loop cannot generate a five-figure bill overnight.

topics.title: Real-time streaming UX: SSE, WebSockets, optimistic UI
topics.explainer: Users judge AI apps by time to first token. Server-Sent Events stream tokens one way over HTTP and suit most chat. WebSockets are two-way and suit voice and collaborative apps. For voice, add voice activity detection and barge-in, which cancels TTS and generation when the user speaks. Stream tool calls too: show 'searching…' as soon as the call is emitted, and render partial JSON arguments carefully. Optimistic UI shows the user's action immediately and reconciles later. Always handle reconnects, cancellation and backpressure.

subtopics.title: SSE vs WebSockets
subtopics.text: SSE is a one-way HTTP stream from server to browser, ideal for tokens; WebSockets are two-way, suited to voice and collaboration.

subtopics.title: Time to first token and perceived latency
Streaming tool calls and partial JSON
subtopics.text: Show tool calls as soon as they start, and only parse partial JSON arguments with a tolerant parser.

subtopics.title: Cancellation and reconnects
subtopics.text: Wire the cancel button to the server so generation stops, and let clients resume a stream after a network drop.

quiz.q: A kill switch should be able to…
choices: Disable tools or force safe mode quickly
quiz.why: Operational safety needs fast containment.

quiz.q: Spend caps per user mainly guard against…
choices: Abuse and runaway loops creating huge bills
quiz.why: Hard limits contain the blast radius.

quiz.q: Tool calls should be authorized against…
quiz.why: Otherwise the agent becomes a confused deputy.

quiz.q: A chat app only needs to stream from server to client over HTTP. What is the simplest fit?
quiz.why: SSE is a simple one-way HTTP stream.

quiz.q: What is barge-in?
choices: Cancelling playback and generation when the user starts speaking
quiz.why: Barge-in lets users interrupt a voice agent.

lesson.intuition: A demo works once on a good day. A product works thousands of times a day, including during provider outages, traffic spikes and attacks. Production hardening adds the boring parts that keep AI features alive: timeouts, fallbacks, queues, observability with costs, security on tools and a streaming UX that feels fast.
how: Reliability: deadlines, circuit breakers, fallback models, queues with backpressure, idempotent writes, load shedding.
Observability: structured traces per request (prompt version, tools, tokens, cost, latency) with PII redaction, and sampled quality scores.
Security: authentication and authorization on every tool, output filtering, dependency pinning, spend caps.
UX: stream tokens and tool progress, support cancel and reconnect.
On-call: alert on quality and cost anomalies, not only on errors.
lesson.example: Circuit breaker: if more than 50% of calls to provider A fail within a 30-second window (minimum 20 calls), open the breaker and send traffic to provider B for 60 seconds, then let a few test requests through (half-open). During a 10-minute outage at 100 requests per second, this avoids roughly 60,000 slow failed calls to A.
mistakes: Logging raw prompts with customer data to a shared logging system.
No kill switch when a prompt change makes an agent loop on tools.
Paging only on HTTP 5xx while answer quality silently drops.
lesson.enterprise: A food-delivery app streams support answers token by token, shows 'checking your order…' when a tool call starts, and falls back to a smaller model when the main provider breaker opens. Traces include cost, so a spike from a looping prompt was spotted and rolled back within 15 minutes.
takeaways: Assume every dependency fails; design the fallback.
Trace tokens and dollars, with redaction.
Stream for perceived speed; alert on quality.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> GW[API + auth]
  GW --> Q[Queue / backpressure]
  Q --> BR{Circuit breaker}
  BR -->|closed| PA[Provider A]
  BR -->|open| PB[Provider B]
  PA --> S[Stream SSE to user]
  PB --> S
  GW --> TR[(Traces: tokens, $, latency, redacted)]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: user requests pass auth and a queue to a circuit breaker that picks provider A or B; responses stream back via SSE and every request is traced with tokens, cost and latency.

subjects.title: Fine-Tuning & Adaptation
subjects.why: Fine-tune when prompting and retrieval hit a ceiling.
subjects.explainer:
SFT for format and style, LoRA/QLoRA for efficient adaptation, DPO-style preference methods when ranked feedback exists. Data quality beats quantity. Watch for catastrophic forgetting and eval before merge. Synthetic data helps if validated against held-out human gold.

Common mistake: fine-tuning to fix retrieval failures. Another: no license review on training data.

Keep a decision record: why fine-tune beat better prompts.

topics.title: Decision

subtopics.title: Prompt/RAG ceiling tests
subtopics.text: Run your eval with the best prompt and retrieval you can build. If they already meet the target, don't fine-tune.

subtopics.title: Forgetting risk
subtopics.text: Narrow fine-tuning can degrade unrelated abilities; keep general tests in the eval suite.

topics.explainer: Fine-tune only after prompts and retrieval hit a ceiling you can measure. Fine-tuning is good at style, format, narrow skills and making smaller models act like bigger ones; it is bad at teaching fresh facts, which RAG handles better. You need clean, representative data, usually hundreds to thousands of examples. Watch for catastrophic forgetting of general skills. Check that the base model's license allows tuning and your use.

topics.title: Methods

subtopics.title: LoRA / QLoRA / DoRA family
subtopics.text: LoRA trains small low-rank matrices added to frozen weights; QLoRA does this on a 4-bit quantized base model to save memory.

subtopics.title: DPO / ORPO / KTO
subtopics.text: DPO learns directly from pairs of preferred and rejected answers without training a separate reward model.

topics.explainer: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains on input-output pairs. LoRA freezes the base model and learns small low-rank matrices, cutting memory and producing swappable adapters; QLoRA does this on a 4-bit base. Preference methods such as DPO, ORPO and KTO learn from chosen-versus-rejected pairs without a separate reward model. Synthetic data can bootstrap training but must be filtered and validated. Always compare the tuned model to the base on your eval suite before merging.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Dataset versioning
subtopics.text: Version training data like code so every fine-tuned model can be traced to the exact dataset.

subtopics.title: Checkpoint selection
subtopics.text: Evaluate several checkpoints, not just the last one, because later checkpoints can overfit.

subtopics.title: Rollback
subtopics.text: Keep the previous model deployable so you can switch back if the new one regresses.

topics.explainer: Version datasets alongside checkpoints. Pick checkpoints by eval score, not by the lowest training loss. Run regression suites that include general capabilities, not just the target task. Keep the previous adapter ready for instant rollback. Budget for refreshes: when the base model gets a new release, you may need to retrain, so automate the pipeline. Try it: keep a one-line rollback command in the runbook and rehearse it, so reverting an adapter takes seconds instead of a meeting.

quiz.q: LoRA adapts models by…
quiz.why: Low-rank adapters are the core idea.

quiz.q: Fine-tuning is a poor choice for…
choices: Distilling a skill into a smaller model
quiz.why: RAG handles fresh facts better; tuning bakes in a snapshot.

quiz.q: DPO trains on…
choices: Pairs of chosen and rejected responses
quiz.why: It optimizes preferences directly without an RL loop.

lesson.intuition: Fine-tuning is extra training on your own examples so a model learns a format, style or narrow skill. It's like on-the-job training after general schooling. It's powerful but often unnecessary: better prompts or better retrieval solve many problems more cheaply. Fine-tune when you've hit their ceiling and have good data.
how: Prove the ceiling: measure the best prompt + RAG setup on your eval set first.
Collect and clean examples: a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality input-output pairs, checked for licensing and PII.
Choose a method: SFT on demonstrations; LoRA or QLoRA for efficient adapters; DPO-style methods when you have preferred vs rejected answers.
Train, then evaluate on a held-out set plus general-capability regression tests.
Version datasets and checkpoints, keep a rollback, and record why fine-tuning beat prompting.
lesson.example: LoRA parameter count: adapting one 4096 × 4096 attention projection with rank r = 16 trains two matrices, 4096 × 16 and 16 × 4096, which is 2 × 65,536 = 131,072 parameters instead of 16.8M, about 0.8%. Applying it to the 4 attention projections in each of 32 layers gives 128 × 131,072 ≈ 16.8M trainable parameters for the whole model.
mistakes: Fine-tuning to fix what is actually a retrieval problem: the model can't learn facts that change weekly.
Training on data you don't have the rights to use.
Skipping general regression tests and causing the model to forget other skills.
lesson.enterprise: An insurer fine-tuned a small open model with LoRA on 3,000 approved claim-summary examples. It matched a much larger API model's quality on their eval at about a tenth of the serving cost, and the adapter can be rolled back in minutes.
takeaways: Prompt and RAG first; fine-tune at the ceiling.
Data quality beats quantity.
LoRA makes adaptation cheap and reversible.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  BASE[Best prompt + RAG] --> EV{Ceiling reached?}
  EV -->|no| ITER[Improve prompt / retrieval]
  EV -->|yes| DATA[Curate examples]
  DATA --> M{Method}
  M --> SFT[SFT]
  M --> LORA[LoRA / QLoRA]
  M --> DPO[DPO]
  SFT --> TEST[Held-out + regression evals]
  LORA --> TEST
  DPO --> TEST
  TEST --> SHIP[Ship with rollback]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: start from the best prompt and RAG; if the ceiling is reached, curate examples, choose SFT, LoRA or DPO, run held-out and regression evals, and ship with rollback.

subjects.title: Synthetic Data & Distillation
subjects.why: Teacher models can mint training fuel — carefully.
subjects.explainer:
Distillation and synthetic data expand scarce labels. Risks: mirroring teacher blind spots, leaking eval contamination, and mode collapse. Prefer diverse generators, critique/filter pipelines, and human spot checks. On-policy data from your own agent traces often beats generic synthetic chat.

Common mistake: training on the same scraped web as the teacher without filters. Another: reporting gains only on synthetic tests.

Always hold out real user-like gold.

subjects.project: Generate synthetic tool-call traces; filter with a critic; train a small student; eval on human gold.

topics.title: Generation

subtopics.title: Diversity controls
subtopics.text: Vary prompts, topics, personas, lengths and difficulty so the data covers the real distribution.

subtopics.title: Critique/filter loops
subtopics.text: Have a model critique or verify each example and discard failures before training.

subtopics.title: On-policy traces
subtopics.text: Your own agent's real traces, corrected by humans, often teach more than generic synthetic chats.

topics.explainer: Synthetic data comes from prompting a strong teacher model to produce examples. Control diversity with varied seeds, personas and topics, or you get thousands of near-duplicates. Filter with critique loops, verifiers, or executable checks such as unit tests. On-policy traces from your own model capture its real mistakes. Check that synthetic items do not overlap your evaluation set, or scores become meaningless.

topics.title: Distillation

subtopics.title: Logit / response distillation
subtopics.text: Logit distillation matches the teacher's full probability distribution; response distillation trains on the teacher's text outputs.

subtopics.title: Failure inheritance
subtopics.text: If the teacher is wrong on a type of input, the student will be too, so test those cases separately.

topics.explainer: Distillation trains a smaller student to imitate a larger teacher. Logit distillation matches the teacher's full output distribution, which carries more signal than single answers; response distillation trains on teacher outputs only and works with API teachers. Task-specific students can be ten times cheaper with similar quality on that task. Students inherit teacher errors and biases. Plan a refresh cadence as teachers improve.

quiz.q: Synthetic data is safest when…
choices: Filtered and validated against held-out human gold
Used as the only test set
quiz.why: Human gold keeps you honest.

quiz.q: Diversity controls in synthetic data generation prevent…
quiz.why: Varied seeds, personas and topics broaden coverage.

quiz.q: Logit distillation carries more signal than response distillation because…
choices: The student sees the teacher's full probability distribution
quiz.why: Soft targets show how the teacher ranks alternatives.

lesson.intuition: Good training data is scarce, so teams ask a strong 'teacher' model to generate examples for a smaller 'student'. Done carefully, synthetic data and distillation let a small, cheap model do one job almost as well as a big one. Done carelessly, the student inherits the teacher's mistakes and your evals become meaningless.
how: Define the target task and a small set of real, human-checked gold examples.
Generate candidates with a teacher model using varied prompts, personas and difficulty levels.
Filter: automatic checks, a critique model and human spot checks remove bad examples.
Train the student (SFT or distillation) and evaluate on held-out real data, not synthetic data.
Check for contamination: synthetic examples must not copy your eval questions.
lesson.example: Filtering yield: you generate 20,000 candidate Q&A pairs. Deduplication removes 15% (17,000 left), schema and fact checks remove 25% of the rest (12,750 left), and a critique model rejects 20% (10,200 left). Human review of a 300-example sample finds 4% still bad, so you expect about 400 bad examples in the final set and decide whether to tighten filters.
mistakes: Reporting gains only on synthetic test sets.
Low diversity: thousands of near-identical examples that teach one narrow pattern.
Ignoring the teacher model's terms of use on training other models.
lesson.enterprise: A customer-support company distills a large model's ticket-classification behavior into a small model using 50,000 synthetic tickets plus 2,000 real labeled ones. On a held-out real set, the student is within 1.5 points of the teacher at a fraction of the latency.
takeaways: Synthetic data needs filters and real held-out gold.
Diversity matters as much as volume.
Students inherit teacher blind spots.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  GOLD[Real gold examples] --> T[Teacher prompts: varied]
  T --> GEN[Generate candidates]
  GEN --> F1[Dedup + checks]
  F1 --> F2[Critique model]
  F2 --> F3[Human spot check]
  F3 --> TRAIN[Train student]
  TRAIN --> EVAL[Eval on held-out real data]
  GOLD --> EVAL
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: real gold examples guide varied teacher prompts; generated candidates pass deduplication, critique and human checks; a student is trained and evaluated on held-out real data.

subjects.title: Multimodal and Document RAG: PDFs, Tables, Charts and Images
subjects.why: Enterprise answers hide in tables, charts and scanned pages; text-only RAG silently fails on them.
subjects.explainer:
Document RAG extends retrieval to the parts of a document that are not running prose. There are two families of approaches.

Parse-then-embed: a layout-aware parser (Docling, Unstructured, Azure Document Intelligence, AWS Textract, LlamaParse) detects headings, tables, figures and reading order. Tables become Markdown or HTML with headers preserved; charts and images get VLM-generated descriptions (and ideally extracted data series); everything is chunked with page and bounding-box references and embedded as text.

Embed-the-page: visual document retrieval models such as ColPali/ColQwen embed page images directly into multi-vector representations and use late interaction (MaxSim) to match query tokens to image patches. No OCR pipeline, strong on charts and complex layouts, but indexes are larger and answers need a VLM that reads the retrieved page images.

Many production systems are hybrid: text retrieval over parsed content plus visual retrieval over pages, fused and reranked, with a VLM generating the answer and citing page regions.

Common mistakes: flattening tables into word soup; ignoring figures; losing page references so answers cannot be cited; sending 40 full-resolution page images to a VLM per question.

Mental model: a PDF is a picture of information. Either turn the picture into faithful structure, or retrieve the picture itself.
