Write 40 questions (15 about tables, 15 about charts, 10 prose) and compare recall@5 and answer accuracy per question type, plus index size and cost.

topics.title: Layout parsing and table/chart extraction
topics.explainer: Layout models detect regions (title, paragraph, table, figure, caption) and reading order, which matters for multi-column pages. Table structure recognition recovers rows, columns and merged headers; serialize tables to Markdown or HTML and keep the header with every chunk of a long table. For charts, a VLM can produce a caption and often the underlying data series as JSON, which makes numbers searchable. Keep page numbers and bounding boxes so citations can highlight the exact region.

subtopics.title: Parsers compared: Docling, Unstructured, LlamaParse, cloud document AI
subtopics.text: Open-source parsers (Docling, Unstructured) and services (LlamaParse, Azure Document Intelligence, AWS Textract, Google Document AI) differ on tables, scans and cost. Test them on your documents.

subtopics.title: Table structure recognition
subtopics.text: Table structure recognition recovers rows, columns and merged headers so values keep their meaning.

subtopics.title: Serializing tables with headers
subtopics.text: Repeat the header row in every chunk of a long table so each chunk is self-explanatory.

topics.title: Visual retrieval with ColPali-style models
topics.explainer: ColPali feeds a page image through a vision-language model and keeps one embedding per image patch, about a thousand vectors per page. A query is embedded per token, and the score is the sum, over query tokens, of the best-matching patch (late interaction, MaxSim). This captures layout, fonts, charts and tables without OCR. The cost is storage and compute: multi-vector indexes are much larger than one-vector-per-chunk indexes, so use token pooling, binarization or a first-stage single-vector filter.

subtopics.title: Patch embeddings and late interaction
subtopics.text: ColPali embeds each image patch and scores a query by matching each query token to its best patch (late interaction).

subtopics.title: When visual retrieval beats parsing
subtopics.text: Visual retrieval shines on slides, charts and complex layouts where parsing loses information.

topics.title: Multimodal embeddings, fusion and generation
topics.explainer: Multimodal embedding models place images and text in one space so a text query can find a photo or diagram. Hybrid systems run text and visual retrieval in parallel, fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, and rerank. Generation uses a VLM that receives the top pages as images plus extracted text, with instructions to cite page and region. Evaluate by question type, because a system that is great on prose can still be poor on charts, and control image count and resolution to manage latency and cost.

subtopics.title: Reciprocal rank fusion
subtopics.text: Reciprocal rank fusion merges ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank) per item, rewarding agreement.

subtopics.title: Image resolution and token budgets
subtopics.text: Higher image resolution means more image tokens, so pick the smallest resolution that keeps text readable.

quiz.q: What does ColPali embed?
choices: Page images as multi-vector patch embeddings
quiz.why: It embeds page images directly with one vector per patch and scores with late interaction.

quiz.q: A long table is split across chunks and answers get columns wrong. Best fix?
choices: Repeat the table header in every chunk of the table
quiz.why: Headers give each chunk the column meaning.

quiz.q: Main trade-off of multi-vector visual indexes?
choices: Much larger storage and scoring cost
quiz.why: Hundreds to thousands of vectors per page increase index size; compress or use two stages.

lesson.intuition: Enterprise knowledge lives in PDFs, slides, scanned forms, tables and charts, not just clean text. Plain text extraction loses table structure and ignores charts, so answers hiding there are never found. Document RAG either parses the layout carefully before indexing, or retrieves page images directly with vision models, and often does both.
how: Parse: a layout-aware parser finds headings, paragraphs, tables, figures and reading order.
Convert tables to Markdown or HTML with headers repeated, and describe charts and images with a vision model.
Chunk with page numbers and bounding boxes so citations can point to the exact region.
Optionally index page images with a ColPali-style model for visual retrieval, and fuse with text retrieval.
Generate with a VLM or LLM that cites page and region, and evaluate by question type (prose, table, chart).
lesson.example: Visual index size: ColPali-style models store about 1,030 patch vectors of 128 dimensions per page. For 100,000 pages in float16: 100,000 × 1,030 × 128 × 2 bytes ≈ 26 GB. Binarizing vectors (1 bit per dimension) cuts that to about 1.6 GB, which is why compression or a first-stage single-vector filter is common.
mistakes: Flattening tables into text so rows and columns get mixed up.
Losing page numbers, so answers can't be cited or verified.
Evaluating only on prose questions when users ask about tables and charts.
lesson.enterprise: An investment firm indexes 10 years of annual reports. Parsing tables with headers preserved and adding chart descriptions raised accuracy on financial-table questions from 52% to 81% on their eval; citations highlight the exact table on the page.
takeaways: Layout matters: parse structure before chunking.
Keep page and box references for citations.
Evaluate per question type.

subjects.title: Vision and Document AI: OCR vs VLM Extraction to Structured Data
subjects.why: Receipts, invoices, IDs and forms drive real workflows; agents need their data as validated JSON, not as a picture.
subjects.explainer:
Document AI turns images and scans into structured records. Classic pipelines run OCR (Tesseract, PaddleOCR, cloud OCR) to get text with coordinates, then rules or a small model map text to fields. Specialized processors (AWS Textract AnalyzeExpense, Azure prebuilt receipt/invoice, Google Document AI) return typed fields with confidence scores.

Vision-language models (GPT-class, Claude, Gemini, Qwen-VL) can read an image and emit JSON directly against a schema using structured outputs. They handle messy layouts and handwriting better than rules, but can hallucinate a plausible total. The robust pattern combines them: VLM or processor extraction into a strict schema, then deterministic validation (line items sum to subtotal, subtotal plus tax equals total, dates parse, currency is known, vendor matches a known list), confidence thresholds, and a human review queue for failures.

Common mistakes: trusting a single extraction without arithmetic checks; storing floats for money; ignoring image quality (blur, rotation, glare); no ground-truth set to measure field accuracy.

Mental model: extraction is a guess; validation turns it into data.

Compare a VLM with structured output against OCR + rules on 50 hand-labeled receipts; report per-field accuracy, validation catch rate and cost per receipt.

topics.title: OCR pipelines and specialized processors
topics.explainer: OCR detects text regions and recognizes characters, returning words with bounding boxes and confidence. Preprocessing (deskew, denoise, contrast, crop) matters as much as the engine for phone photos. Specialized cloud processors add document understanding on top: they know where totals and tax usually sit and return normalized fields. They are fast, cheap per page and give confidence scores, but only for supported document types and languages.

subtopics.title: Image preprocessing
subtopics.text: Fixing rotation, contrast and skew before extraction often improves accuracy more than changing the model.

subtopics.title: Prebuilt receipt and invoice processors
subtopics.text: Cloud services such as Textract AnalyzeExpense or Azure prebuilt invoice models return typed fields with confidence scores.

topics.title: VLM extraction with structured outputs
topics.explainer: Give the VLM the image, a JSON schema and field definitions, and use structured-output mode so the response always parses. Ask for null rather than guesses when a field is unreadable, and for the source text of each value to aid review. Downscale images to the smallest resolution that preserves legibility to control tokens. VLMs generalize to new layouts without templates, which makes them the fastest way to cover long-tail documents.

subtopics.title: Schema-constrained JSON
subtopics.text: Ask the model for JSON matching a schema so extracted fields are machine-checkable.

subtopics.title: Null instead of guessing
subtopics.text: Tell the model to return null when a field isn't visible; a missing value is safer than an invented one.

subtopics.title: Resolution and token cost
subtopics.text: Higher image resolution improves small-text reading but costs more tokens per page.

topics.title: Validation, confidence and human review
topics.explainer: Validate every record deterministically: arithmetic (line items sum to subtotal, subtotal plus tax equals total), formats (dates, currency codes), ranges and reference data (known vendors, tax rates). Store money as integer cents or decimals, never floats. Route records that fail validation or have low confidence to a review queue, and feed corrections back into the eval set. Measure field-level accuracy and straight-through processing rate, the share of documents needing no human touch.

subtopics.title: Decimal money handling
subtopics.text: Use integer minor units (cents) or decimal types for money, never binary floats.

subtopics.title: Straight-through processing rate
subtopics.text: Straight-through processing rate is the share of documents that need no human touch, a key business metric.

quiz.q: A VLM returns a receipt total that does not equal its line items plus tax. Which check catches this?
quiz.why: Deterministic arithmetic checks catch inconsistent extractions.

quiz.q: How should money be stored?
quiz.why: Floats introduce rounding errors.

quiz.q: What does straight-through processing rate measure?
choices: Share of documents processed with no human review
quiz.why: It is the key automation metric for document AI.

lesson.intuition: Many business processes start with a picture: a receipt, an invoice, an ID card, a form. The goal is not to describe the picture but to turn it into trustworthy data, such as a vendor name, a date and a total that adds up. Vision models make extraction flexible, and validation rules make it reliable.
how: Preprocess the image: rotate, deskew, check resolution and blur.
Extract with OCR plus rules, a prebuilt document processor, or a VLM with a strict JSON schema.
Allow null for missing fields instead of guessing, and capture evidence (text or box) for each field.
Validate: arithmetic (line items sum to subtotal, subtotal + tax = total), formats, known vendors, currency.
Route failures or low-confidence fields to human review and track the straight-through processing rate.
lesson.example: Validation catches a hallucination: a VLM reads a receipt as subtotal 42.50, tax 3.40, total 48.90. The check 42.50 + 3.40 = 45.90 ≠ 48.90 fails, so the receipt goes to review. A human sees the total is actually 45.90 (the model misread a 5 as an 8). Storing amounts as integer cents (4250 + 340 = 4590) avoids floating-point rounding issues.
mistakes: Trusting one extraction without arithmetic or format checks.
Storing money as floating-point numbers.
Testing only on clean scans when users send blurry phone photos.
lesson.enterprise: An accounts-payable team processes 40,000 invoices a month. A prebuilt invoice processor handles common layouts, a VLM handles the long tail, and validation rules send 8% to human review. Straight-through processing rose from 35% to 78%.
takeaways: Extraction is a guess; validation makes it data.
Prefer null to a plausible guess.
Measure straight-through rate and field accuracy.

subjects.title: Multi-Model Routing & Ensembles
subjects.why: Route cheap to expensive; specialize by task.
subjects.explainer:
Heuristic or learned routers, confidence/entropy signals, cascades, and verifiers reduce spend. Best-of-N and critique patterns trade cost for quality. Keep A/B assignment honest.

Common mistake: a router trained on demos that never sees production dialects. Another: cascades without a hard cost ceiling.

Measure dollars and quality together on the same slices.

resources.why: LiteLLM gateway documentation; concrete configuration for routing, budgets and fallbacks.

topics.title: Routing

subtopics.title: Heuristic vs learned
subtopics.text: Heuristic routers use rules (length, keywords); learned routers are classifiers trained on which model succeeded for past requests.

subtopics.title: Confidence / entropy
subtopics.text: Low token probabilities or high entropy in the cheap model's answer can signal it should escalate.

subtopics.title: Cascade and deferral
subtopics.text: A cascade tries models in order of cost and stops at the first acceptable answer.

topics.explainer: Routing sends each request to the cheapest model likely to handle it. Heuristic routers use rules (length, keywords, user tier); learned routers predict difficulty from features. Confidence signals such as logprob entropy or a verifier score can trigger escalation. Cascades try a small model first and defer to a larger one when unsure. Run A/B assignment to measure the quality and cost effect of every routing change.

topics.title: Ensembles

subtopics.title: Best-of-N
subtopics.text: Generate N answers and keep the one a verifier scores highest. Cost grows about linearly with N.

subtopics.title: Verifier models
subtopics.text: A verifier can be code (tests, schema), a rule set or a judge model that checks the answer.

topics.explainer: Ensembles spend more compute for quality. Best-of-N samples several answers and picks the best with a scorer. Verifier models check answers, which works especially well when correctness is checkable (code, math). Debate and critique loops have models review each other. Cap cost per request and keep latency inside the SLO, because ensembles multiply both quickly. Try it: on 100 hard cases, compare single-shot accuracy with best-of-5 plus a verifier, and compute the cost per extra correct answer.

quiz.q: A cascade should…
choices: Stop at the first model that meets a confidence policy
quiz.why: Early exit is the point.

quiz.q: A cascade router escalates to a larger model when…
choices: The small model is uncertain or fails a check
quiz.why: Confidence signals or verifiers trigger deferral.

quiz.q: Best-of-N works best when…
choices: A reliable scorer or verifier exists
quiz.why: Picking the best needs a way to recognize it.

lesson.intuition: Not every question needs your most expensive model. Routing sends easy requests to cheap models and hard ones to strong models, like a hospital triage desk. Ensembles go the other way: spend more on hard cases by sampling several answers and picking the best with a verifier. Both are ways to buy quality where it matters and save money where it doesn't.
how: Collect signals: request features (length, topic), a small classifier, or the cheap model's own confidence.
Route: rules or a learned router choose a model; a cascade tries cheap first and escalates on low confidence or verifier failure.
For hard cases, use best-of-N sampling with a verifier (tests, schema, judge) or a critique step.
Cap cost and latency per request so cascades and ensembles can't run away.
Evaluate quality and cost together on the same slices, with honest A/B assignment.
lesson.example: Cascade economics: 1M requests at 1,500 tokens. Always large at $5 per 1M tokens: 1.5B tokens → $7,500. Cascade: all go to small at $0.30 per 1M ($450), and 20% escalate to large (300M tokens → $1,500). Total $1,950, a 74% saving, as long as routed quality stays within your threshold.
mistakes: Training a router on demo prompts that don't look like production traffic.
Cascades with no cost ceiling, so hard requests try every model.
Comparing models on different traffic slices and calling it an A/B test.
lesson.enterprise: A coding-help product sends autocomplete to a small fast model, chat questions to a mid model, and failing-test fixes to a reasoning model with best-of-3 and the test suite as verifier. Cost per active user fell 45% with higher fix rates.
takeaways: Route cheap first; escalate on evidence.
Verifiers make best-of-N worth it.
Always cap cost and latency.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  R[Request] --> RT{Router}
  RT -->|easy| S[Small model]
  RT -->|hard| L[Large model]
  S --> V{Verifier}
  V -->|pass| OUT[Answer]
  V -->|fail| L
  L --> BON[Best-of-N + verifier]
  BON --> OUT
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a router sends easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a large model; small-model answers that fail a verifier escalate, and the large model can use best-of-N with a verifier.

subjects.title: Data Flywheels
subjects.why: Production traffic is training fuel if you instrument it.
subjects.explainer:
Capture consenting, redacted traces; mine failures; queue active learning. Feed eval expansion, SFT, and preference pairs. Close the loop weekly.

Common mistake: storing everything forever without redaction. Another: never promoting production failures into the golden set.

Flywheels need product and legal buy-in, not only ML enthusiasm.

subjects.project: Thumbs and tool-success signals → weekly curated fine-tune and eval delta sets.

topics.title: Capture

subtopics.title: Consent and redaction
subtopics.text: Get user and legal consent for using interactions to improve the product, and strip personal data before storage.

subtopics.title: Sampling bias
subtopics.text: Users who give feedback are not a random sample; weigh this when interpreting feedback rates.

topics.explainer: A data flywheel turns usage into improvement. Capture traces only with consent and redaction in place. Mine failures from explicit feedback, user edits, retries and escalations. Use active learning to queue the most informative examples for labeling. Watch sampling bias: users who give feedback are not representative, and you will over-fit to them if you are careless. Try it: list every signal your app already emits (edits, retries, copies, thumbs) and rank them by how strongly they indicate failure.

topics.title: Use

subtopics.title: Eval expansion
subtopics.text: Every confirmed production failure should become a test case so it never silently returns.

subtopics.title: SFT / preference pairs
subtopics.text: Good outputs become fine-tuning demonstrations; pairs of preferred and rejected outputs become preference data.

subtopics.title: Prompt regressions
subtopics.text: Turn past failures into test cases so prompt changes can't silently reintroduce them.

topics.explainer: Captured data feeds several loops: new eval cases, SFT examples, preference pairs from edited or rejected answers, reward signals for RL, and regression tests for prompts. Publish a regular quality report that shows how the flywheel moved key metrics. A flywheel that only collects data without changing the product is just storage cost. Try it: every week, turn the top five new failure clusters into eval cases before anyone changes a prompt. This keeps fixes honest.

topics.title: DPO feedback flywheel end to end
topics.explainer: A preference flywheel turns user feedback into training data. Log every response with the prompt, context and model version. When a user gives a thumbs-down and then accepts an edited or regenerated answer, that pair becomes a chosen and rejected example. Filter the pairs for PII, spam and label noise, deduplicate, and hold out an eval split. A nightly job trains a LoRA adapter with DPO, and the adapter is promoted only if offline evals and a shadow or canary test beat the current version.

subtopics.title: Turning thumbs-down and edits into preference pairs
subtopics.text: A thumbs-down followed by an accepted regeneration or edit gives a natural rejected/chosen pair.

subtopics.title: Eval gates, shadow and canary promotion
subtopics.text: Promote a new adapter only if it beats the current one on offline evals and in a shadow or canary test.

quiz.q: A flywheel without redaction…
quiz.why: Traces often contain secrets and PII.

quiz.q: User edits to a draft are valuable because they…
quiz.why: Original vs edited is a chosen/rejected pair.

quiz.q: The main sampling risk in feedback data is…
quiz.why: Bias toward vocal users skews training and evals.

quiz.q: What does a DPO training example contain?
choices: A prompt plus a chosen and a rejected response
quiz.why: DPO learns from preference pairs.

quiz.q: When should a nightly adapter be promoted?
choices: Only after it beats the current model on offline evals and a shadow or canary test
quiz.why: Gates prevent regressions.

lesson.intuition: A data flywheel turns everyday usage into improvements. Each interaction can produce evidence: a thumbs-down, an edit, an escalation. Captured carefully, that evidence grows your eval set, finds failure patterns and becomes training data, which makes the product better, which brings more usage. It needs consent, redaction and discipline to spin safely.
how: Capture consented, redacted traces: prompt, context, tool calls, output, model and prompt versions, feedback.
Mine failures: cluster low-rated or escalated interactions and label root causes.
Promote real failures into the golden eval set.
Build training data: corrected answers for SFT, chosen/rejected pairs for DPO.
Retrain or re-prompt, gate on evals, and repeat on a regular cadence.
lesson.example: From feedback to pairs: in a month, 200,000 answers get 6,000 thumbs-downs. In 2,500 of those, the user regenerated and accepted a new answer, giving 2,500 candidate chosen/rejected pairs. After PII scrubbing, deduplication and removing noisy or spammy feedback (30%), 1,750 pairs remain, enough for a small DPO run on a LoRA adapter.
mistakes: Storing everything forever without consent or redaction.
Never promoting production failures into the eval set.
Training on raw feedback without filtering noise and abuse.
lesson.enterprise: A writing-assistant product reviews the top 5 failure clusters every week. Each fix ships with new eval cases from those clusters, and accepted user edits feed a monthly preference-tuning run.
takeaways: Instrument for learning from day one.
Failures become evals first, training data second.
Consent, redaction and filtering are non-negotiable.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  USE[Usage] --> CAP[Capture redacted traces + feedback]
  CAP --> MINE[Mine failure clusters]
  MINE --> EVAL[Grow eval set]
  MINE --> PAIRS[SFT data + DPO pairs]
  PAIRS --> TRAIN[Train / re-prompt]
  EVAL --> GATE{Eval gate}
  TRAIN --> GATE
  GATE --> SHIP[Ship] --> USE
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: usage is captured as redacted traces and feedback, failures are mined into eval cases and training pairs, training is gated by evals, and shipped improvements bring more usage.

subjects.title: On-Device & Edge Apps
subjects.why: Local models change latency, privacy, and UX.
subjects.explainer:
GGUF/llama.cpp, MLX, ExecuTorch, NPUs, and hybrid local+cloud patterns matter. Cold start, memory budgets, update channels, and honest privacy UX copy are product work.

Common mistake: promising fully offline while still shipping telemetry that needs network. Another: a 7B model that jetsams the OS on mid phones.

Benchmark on target devices, not only your MacBook.

resources.title: llama.cpp
resources.why: Source repository: read the README and examples to see how it is used in practice.

resources.title: Hugging Face LLM Course
resources.why: Free hands-on course chapters with code; good first practical exposure.

resources.title: PyTorch tutorials
resources.why: Official PyTorch documentation or tutorial with runnable code.

subjects.project: Local RAG demo with llama.cpp or similar; compare quality/latency to cloud on 20 queries.

topics.title: Stack

subtopics.title: GGUF / quantized runtimes
subtopics.text: GGUF is the file format used by llama.cpp for quantized models, commonly at 4-8 bits per weight.

subtopics.title: Memory budgets
subtopics.text: Total memory is weights plus KV cache plus runtime overhead; long contexts grow the KV cache.

topics.explainer: Edge apps run quantized models (GGUF via llama.cpp, MLX, ONNX Runtime, Core ML, or vendor NPU runtimes) on CPUs, GPUs or NPUs. Memory is the binding constraint: a 7B model at 4-bit is about 4 GB, before KV cache. Hybrid designs keep simple or private tasks local and send hard ones to the cloud. Plan model update channels with signatures and delta downloads, since models are large.

topics.title: UX

subtopics.title: Cold start
subtopics.text: Loading a model from storage takes time. Load lazily, keep it warm when appropriate, and show progress.

subtopics.title: Privacy copy
subtopics.text: Tell users plainly what stays on the device and what may be sent to the cloud.

topics.explainer: On-device AI has UX costs. The first load of a model can take seconds. Offline mode should degrade gracefully rather than fail. Tell users plainly what stays on device and what goes to the cloud. Provide degraded modes on low battery or thermal throttling. Measure battery impact; a feature that drains the phone gets uninstalled. Try it: measure cold-start time and battery drain for ten minutes of use on a mid-range phone, not just a flagship.

quiz.q: Edge deployments most improve…
choices: Privacy and latency for suitable workloads
quiz.why: Fit the workload to the device.

quiz.q: A 7B model quantized to 4 bits needs roughly how much memory for weights?
quiz.why: 7B × 0.5 bytes ≈ 3.5 GB plus some overhead.

quiz.q: Hybrid edge designs typically…
choices: Keep simple or private tasks local and escalate hard ones
quiz.why: They balance privacy, latency and capability.

lesson.intuition: Running a model on the user's own device means no network round trip, no per-token bill and data that never leaves the phone or laptop. The price is a much smaller model, tight memory, battery use and a harder update story. Edge AI works best for narrow, frequent tasks, often with the cloud as a backup for harder ones.
how: Pick a small model and quantize it (for example to 4-bit GGUF) to fit the device's memory.
Choose a runtime for the hardware: llama.cpp, MLX on Apple silicon, ExecuTorch or vendor NPU SDKs.
Budget memory: weights + KV cache + app, below what the OS allows.
Design hybrid behavior: local first, cloud fallback with user consent for harder requests.
Ship updates for models and prompts safely, and test on real target devices.
lesson.example: Memory check: a 3B-parameter model at 4-bit is about 3e9 × 0.5 bytes = 1.5 GB of weights (plus some overhead, call it ~1.8 GB). On a phone with 8 GB RAM where an app can realistically use 2-3 GB, it fits with a small KV cache; a 7B model at 4-bit (~3.5-4 GB) would likely be killed by the OS on mid-range phones.
mistakes: Promising 'fully offline' while telemetry or features still need the network.
Testing only on a developer laptop instead of mid-range target devices.
Ignoring battery and thermal throttling during long generations.
lesson.enterprise: A field-service app runs a small on-device model to summarize technician notes and search manuals offline in basements with no signal. When connectivity returns, complex diagnostic questions can be sent to a cloud model with the technician's consent.
takeaways: Small + quantized + narrow task = good edge fit.
Budget memory for weights and KV cache.
Hybrid local/cloud with honest privacy copy.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U[User request] --> LOC[On-device model: 4-bit]
  LOC --> C{Confident / in scope?}
  C -->|yes| OUT[Answer locally]
  C -->|no| CONSENT{User consents?}
  CONSENT -->|yes| CLOUD[Cloud model]
  CONSENT -->|no| DEG[Degraded answer]
  CLOUD --> OUT
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a request goes to an on-device 4-bit model; if it isn't confident, the app asks for consent to use a cloud model or returns a degraded answer.

subjects.title: AI Platform and LLMOps for Agents
subjects.why: Without a shared platform every team rebuilds gateways, prompt management, evals and tracing; the platform team makes the right way the easy way.
subjects.explainer:
An AI Platform / LLMOps Engineer builds the paved road for agent teams: an LLM gateway (routing, keys, budgets, fallbacks, caching), registries for prompts, models, tools and agents, an eval service wired into CI/CD, tracing and cost attribution, guardrail services, secrets and identity integration, and templates that bootstrap a compliant agent in minutes.

LLMOps differs from classic MLOps: most teams consume models rather than train them, so the versioned artifacts are prompts, tool definitions, retrieval configs and agent graphs, and the release process is driven by evals rather than training metrics. Releases should be declarative: a manifest pins model alias, prompt version, tool versions and policies, promoted through environments with canaries.

Common mistakes: platform built before any product needs it; mandating one framework for everything; no self-service, so the platform team becomes a ticket queue; prompts edited live in a UI with no versioning or review.

Mental model: the platform is a product whose customers are agent teams; measure it by their time-to-production and incident rate.

topics.title: Gateways and registries
topics.explainer: The gateway centralizes model access: one API for many providers, per-team keys, budgets and rate limits, fallbacks, caching, logging and policy hooks. Registries track versioned artifacts: prompts with templates and variables, model aliases mapped to concrete versions, tool definitions and MCP servers, and agent manifests. Keep registries Git-backed or API-backed with review, so every production behavior traces to a reviewed version.

subtopics.title: Model aliases and pinning
subtopics.text: A model alias such as 'support-default' points at a pinned version, so you can change models in one place with an eval run.

subtopics.title: Agent manifests
subtopics.text: An agent manifest lists the prompt, tool, model and policy versions that make up one releasable agent.

topics.title: CI/CD driven by evals
topics.explainer: An agent release is a manifest change. CI runs unit tests, policy checks and the eval suite, comparing against the current production baseline with significance thresholds. CD promotes through environments, canaries a small traffic share with online evals and SLO monitoring, and rolls back automatically on regression. Store eval results with the release so audits and incident reviews can see exactly what was known at release time.

subtopics.title: Eval gates with baselines
subtopics.text: Compare each candidate release with the current baseline on the eval suite and block it if key metrics drop.

subtopics.title: Automatic rollback
subtopics.text: If online metrics regress during a canary, automatically route traffic back to the previous version.

topics.title: Self-service and developer experience
topics.explainer: Platform success is measured by adoption. Provide templates that generate a repo with tracing, evals, policy config and deployment already wired; a portal listing models, tools, data products and their docs; and clear golden paths for common patterns. Track time-to-first-staging, eval coverage and incident rates per team. Offer escape hatches for advanced teams while keeping security and cost controls mandatory.

subtopics.title: Project templates
subtopics.text: Starter templates give teams a working project with logging, evals and security already wired in.

subtopics.title: Golden paths
subtopics.text: A golden path is the supported, documented way to build and ship, making the safe way the easy way.

subtopics.title: Mandatory vs optional controls
subtopics.text: Decide which controls every project must use (auth, logging) and which are recommended.

topics.title: Graceful degradation and fallback chains
topics.explainer: Plan for outages, rate limits and budget overruns before they happen. A fallback chain tries a frontier model, then a mid-tier model, then a local model, then a semantic cache or a canned answer. Each step triggers on errors, timeouts or a budget signal. Cost kill switches watch spend per tenant and per feature, and step down tiers or disable expensive features at thresholds. Tell users when quality is degraded, log which tier served each request, and test the chain with chaos drills.

subtopics.title: Fallback chain: frontier, mid, local, cache
Triggers: errors, timeouts, rate limits, budget
subtopics.text: Fall back on errors, timeouts, rate limits or budget thresholds, and log which tier served each request.

subtopics.title: Cost kill switches per tenant and feature
Degraded-mode UX messaging
subtopics.text: Tell users when answers come from a reduced mode so they can calibrate trust.

quiz.q: In LLMOps, what is typically the versioned release artifact?
choices: A manifest of model alias, prompt, tools and policies
quiz.why: Agent behavior depends on several versioned components pinned together.

quiz.q: What should gate promotion of an agent release?
choices: Eval results versus baseline plus policy checks
quiz.why: Evals are the release criteria for AI behavior.

quiz.q: How is a platform team best measured?
choices: Agent teams' time-to-production and incident rates
quiz.why: Platform value shows in its customers' outcomes.

quiz.q: Frontier and mid-tier providers fail independently, 2% and 1% of the time. How often are both down?
Which signal should step traffic down to a cheaper tier even when nothing is failing?
choices: A budget threshold from a cost kill switch
quiz.why: Budget triggers enforce FinOps limits.

lesson.intuition: LLMOps is the platform work that lets many teams ship agents safely without each one reinventing the plumbing. Most teams don't train models; they combine prompts, tools, retrieval and model choices. So the versioned, tested, deployable artifacts are those combinations, released through eval gates, watched in production and able to degrade gracefully when things break.
how: Provide a gateway with model aliases, keys, budgets, fallbacks and caching.
Keep registries for prompts, tools/MCP servers and agent manifests, with owners and versions.
Release through CI/CD with eval gates against baselines, then canary with online evals and automatic rollback.
Store release evidence: eval results, approvals and versions.
Define fallback chains and cost kill switches, and test them with chaos drills.
lesson.example: Fallback chain math: 1B tokens a month all on a frontier model at $10 per 1M costs $10,000. In degraded mode after an 80% budget alert: 30% cache hits ($0), 50% mid-tier at $1 per 1M ($500), 20% frontier for critical features ($2,000), total $2,500. If the frontier provider is down 2% of the time and the mid-tier provider 1%, independently, both are down 0.02 × 0.01 = 0.02% of the time.
mistakes: Pinning nothing, so a provider's silent model update changes behavior.
Releasing prompt changes without eval gates because 'it's just text'.
Fallbacks that were never tested and fail when needed.
lesson.enterprise: A bank's platform team offers an agent template: gateway access with model aliases, a prompt registry, an eval CI job and a canary deploy. A prompt change that increased refusals by 8% was rolled back automatically within 20 minutes of canary.
takeaways: Version the whole agent: prompts, tools, models, configs.
Eval gates and canaries for every release.
Plan and drill degradation.

subjects.title: Real-Time Voice Agents: STT, TTS, Turn-Taking and Telephony
subjects.why: Voice is the most natural agent interface and the least forgiving: a second of silence feels broken.
subjects.explainer:
A voice agent listens, decides and speaks in real time. Two architectures dominate.

Cascaded: streaming speech-to-text (Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Whisper variants) → LLM with tools → streaming text-to-speech (ElevenLabs, Cartesia, others). Each stage is swappable and inspectable, and you can use any LLM and tool stack.

Speech-to-speech: a single realtime model (OpenAI Realtime API, Gemini Live and similar) takes audio in and produces audio out, preserving tone and cutting latency, with less control over each stage.

Either way the hard parts are conversational: voice activity detection (VAD) and turn detection decide when the user has finished; barge-in lets the user interrupt and must stop TTS instantly and truncate the agent's context to what was actually spoken; backchannels and fillers mask tool latency. Everything streams: partial transcripts, token streaming into TTS sentence by sentence, audio chunks over WebRTC or WebSockets.

Telephony adds SIP trunks or providers like Twilio, 8 kHz audio, DTMF, call transfer to humans, and recording consent. Frameworks such as LiveKit Agents and Pipecat handle the plumbing.

Common mistakes: waiting for full LLM output before speaking; fixed silence timeouts that cut people off; no barge-in; tools that take 4 seconds with no filler.

Mental model: a voice agent is a latency budget with a personality.

topics.title: Cascaded vs speech-to-speech
topics.explainer: Cascaded pipelines give control: best-in-class STT for accents, any LLM with tools and guardrails, a branded TTS voice, and text transcripts for evals and audits. The cost is latency stacking across three services. Speech-to-speech models collapse the pipeline, respond faster and carry prosody and emotion, but limit model choice and make text-level guardrails and logging harder. Many teams start cascaded for control, then move latency-critical flows to realtime models.

subtopics.title: Cascaded STT → LLM → TTS
subtopics.text: Each stage can be swapped and inspected, and you keep full control of the LLM and tools.

subtopics.title: Speech-to-speech realtime models
subtopics.text: A single model takes audio in and produces audio out, keeping tone and reducing latency, with less control over each step.

topics.title: Turn-taking, VAD and barge-in
topics.explainer: VAD classifies audio frames as speech or silence; turn detection decides whether a pause means the user is done, increasingly using small semantic models on the partial transcript instead of fixed silence timers. Barge-in: when the user starts speaking during agent speech, stop TTS within about 200 ms, cancel pending generation, and record only the words actually played into context so the agent does not believe it said things the user never heard. Echo cancellation prevents the agent hearing itself.

subtopics.title: Voice activity detection
subtopics.text: VAD detects when someone is speaking, based on audio energy and learned patterns.

subtopics.title: Semantic end-of-turn detection
subtopics.text: Semantic end-of-turn models look at what was said to tell a pause from a finished thought.

topics.title: Streaming, latency budget and telephony
topics.explainer: Target roughly 800 ms or less from end of user speech to first agent audio. Budget each hop: end-of-turn detection, final transcript, LLM time to first token, first TTS audio, and network. Stream everything and start TTS on the first sentence. Mask slow tools with short fillers. For phone calls, connect via SIP trunk or Twilio Media Streams, handle 8 kHz mu-law audio, DTMF input, warm transfer to humans, recording disclosures and call-level analytics.

subtopics.title: Voice-to-voice latency budget
subtopics.text: Add up each stage's delay and target well under a second from the user stopping to the agent starting to speak.

subtopics.title: SIP, Twilio and 8 kHz audio
subtopics.text: Phone audio is narrowband (8 kHz), which lowers transcription accuracy; test with real call audio.

quiz.q: The user interrupts the agent mid-sentence. What must happen to the agent's context?
choices: Truncate to the words actually spoken before the interruption
quiz.why: Otherwise the agent believes the user heard things they did not.

quiz.q: Biggest latency win in a cascaded pipeline?
choices: Streaming LLM tokens into TTS sentence by sentence
quiz.why: Starting TTS on the first sentence avoids waiting for the full reply.

quiz.q: Why use semantic end-of-turn detection instead of a fixed silence timer?
choices: It avoids cutting off users who pause mid-thought while staying responsive
quiz.why: Pauses do not always mean the turn is over.

lesson.intuition: A voice agent has to listen, think and speak fast enough to feel like a conversation. People notice gaps longer than about a second. So voice is mostly a latency and turn-taking problem: knowing when the user has finished, starting to speak before the whole answer is ready, and stopping instantly when the user interrupts.
how: Choose an architecture: cascaded (streaming speech-to-text → LLM with tools → streaming text-to-speech) or a speech-to-speech realtime model.
Detect speech and end of turn with voice activity detection and, ideally, a semantic end-of-turn model.
Stream: send partial transcripts, stream LLM tokens and start TTS at the first sentence.
Handle barge-in: when the user speaks, stop audio, cancel generation and trim context to what was actually spoken.
Integrate telephony (SIP, Twilio media streams at 8 kHz), transfers, DTMF and consent notices.
lesson.example: Latency budget for a cascaded agent: end-of-turn detection 300 ms + final STT 150 ms + LLM time to first token 400 ms + time to first sentence 200 ms + TTS time to first audio 150 ms + network 100 ms = 1,300 ms. To get under 1 s, shorten end-of-turn delay with a semantic model, use a faster LLM, and start TTS on the first clause.
mistakes: Waiting for the full LLM answer before starting TTS.
No barge-in, so the agent talks over the user.
Keeping the unspoken part of an interrupted answer in context, so the agent thinks it said things it didn't.
lesson.enterprise: A clinic's appointment line uses a cascaded voice agent with tools for calendar lookup. It plays a short filler ('Let me check that') when a tool call takes longer than 700 ms, transfers to staff on request, and keeps transcripts for quality review with patient consent.
takeaways: Latency and turn-taking decide whether voice feels natural.
Stream every stage; start speaking early.
Barge-in must cancel audio, generation and context.

subjects.why: Speak research-engineer when prompting is not enough.
subjects.explainer:
Map SFT to preference to RL (RLHF/RLAIF, DPO, GRPO, env-based RL). Understand harness overfitting, reward hacking, and contamination. Know when to request a training run versus change the product.

Common mistake: asking for RL to fix a tool schema bug. Another: optimizing a proxy reward that the agent games.

Bring clean env definitions and evals to the training conversation.

topics.title: Methods Map

subtopics.title: RLHF / RLAIF
subtopics.text: RLHF trains a reward model on human comparisons and optimizes the policy against it; RLAIF uses AI feedback instead of humans.

subtopics.title: GRPO and env RL
subtopics.text: GRPO compares a group of sampled answers per prompt and uses their relative rewards, avoiding a separate value network.

topics.explainer: Post-training turns a base model into an assistant. SFT teaches format and behavior from demonstrations. Preference learning, via RLHF with a reward model or RLAIF with AI feedback, teaches which answers people prefer. DPO, ORPO and KTO do preference learning directly from pairs without the RL loop. GRPO and environment-based RL reward verifiable success, such as passing tests. Distillation copies a stronger model's behavior, often cheaper than RL for narrow goals.

topics.title: Risks

subtopics.title: Reward hacking
subtopics.text: Reward hacking is when the model finds a way to get high reward without doing the task, such as editing the tests.

subtopics.title: When not to train
subtopics.text: If the problem is missing data, a bad tool or unclear instructions, fix that instead of training.

topics.explainer: Training can make things worse. Models over-fit to the harness or eval used in training. Reward hacking finds loopholes, such as editing tests instead of fixing code. Entropy collapse makes outputs repetitive and kills exploration. Contaminated evals hide all of this. Often the right call is not to train at all and instead improve prompts, retrieval or tools. Try it: before approving a training run, write down which prompt, retrieval or tool change you tried first and why it was not enough.

topics.title: Post-training pipeline end to end
topics.explainer: A typical post-training pipeline runs supervised fine-tuning on curated demonstrations, then preference optimization (DPO or RLHF with a reward model), then reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for reasoning and tool use, often with GRPO. Each stage needs held-out evals for capability and safety regressions. Pretraining checkpoints set the ceiling; post-training shapes behavior. Track data provenance throughout, and compare every stage against the previous checkpoint and a prompting baseline.

subtopics.title: SFT on demonstrations
subtopics.text: Supervised fine-tuning trains the model on example conversations showing the desired behavior.

subtopics.title: Preference optimization: DPO and RLHF
subtopics.text: DPO trains directly on preferred vs rejected pairs; RLHF trains a reward model and optimizes against it.

subtopics.title: RL with verifiable rewards
subtopics.text: Verifiable rewards come from checks like unit tests passing or an exact answer match.

quiz.q: Reward hacking means…
choices: Optimizing the proxy without true task success
quiz.why: The agent games the metric.

quiz.q: GRPO-style RL is especially effective when…
choices: Rewards are verifiable, like passing tests
quiz.why: Verifiable rewards give clean training signals.

quiz.q: Entropy collapse in RL shows up as…
quiz.why: The policy over-concentrates on a few behaviors.

lesson.intuition: Post-training is what turns a raw pretrained model into a helpful assistant or a strong agent. It usually runs in stages: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, preference optimization from human or AI comparisons, and reinforcement learning on tasks with checkable answers. Application engineers don't need to run it alone, but they need to speak the language and bring clean environments and evals.
how: SFT: train on high-quality demonstrations of the desired behavior.
Preference optimization: RLHF with a reward model and PPO, or direct methods such as DPO, using chosen/rejected pairs.
RL with verifiable rewards: run the model on tasks (math, code, tool use) and reward correct outcomes, often with GRPO.
Evaluate every stage for capability gains and safety or general-skill regressions.
Decide whether training is the right fix at all, versus changing the product, prompt or tool.
lesson.example: GRPO's group-relative advantage: for one prompt the model samples 4 answers with rewards [1, 0, 0, 1]. Mean = 0.5, standard deviation = 0.5. Advantages = (r − mean)/std = [+1, −1, −1, +1]. Correct answers are pushed up and wrong ones down, without training a separate value model.
mistakes: Asking for RL to fix what is really a tool-schema or prompt bug.
Optimizing a proxy reward that the model learns to game.
Evaluating on data that leaked into training.
lesson.enterprise: An enterprise software company works with its model provider on reinforcement fine-tuning for a code-migration agent. It supplies 2,000 tasks in a sandbox with test suites as rewards, plus held-out tasks for evaluation; pass rate on held-out tasks rose from 41% to 63%.
takeaways: SFT → preferences → RL with verifiable rewards.
Rewards get gamed; audit trajectories.
Often the right fix isn't training.

flowchart LR

  SFT --> PREF[Preference optimization: DPO / RLHF]
  PREF --> RL[RL with verifiable rewards: GRPO]
  RL --> EV[Capability + safety evals]
  EV --> REL[Release]

subjects.title: Multimodal Product Engineering
subjects.why: Images, PDFs, and audio change the application contract.
subjects.explainer:
Document AI, screenshot agents, and voice wraps need parsers, size limits, malware scanning, and modality-specific evals. Do not send binaries to a VLM when text extraction suffices.

Common mistake: no max upload or MIME allowlist. Another: evaluating only on clean digital PDFs when users send photos of pages.

Design modality gates in the API, not only in the prompt.

topics.title: Pipelines

subtopics.title: PDF/OCR first
subtopics.text: Try text extraction or OCR first; it is cheaper and easier to cite than sending page images.

subtopics.title: Size and MIME gates
subtopics.text: Reject files that are too large or of unexpected types before any processing.

topics.explainer: Multimodal pipelines should use the cheapest reliable path first: extract text from PDFs and run OCR, and send page images to a VLM only for charts, handwriting or layout-heavy pages. Speech goes through STT before an LLM unless latency demands a native audio model. Screenshots power UI understanding and computer-use agents. Gate inputs by size and MIME type to control cost and attack surface.

topics.title: Eval and Safety

subtopics.title: Modality-specific gold
subtopics.text: Build gold sets per modality, with the real quality and variety users send.

subtopics.title: Prompt injection in pixels
subtopics.text: Text hidden in images (tiny, faint or in screenshots) can carry instructions; never let it change permissions.

topics.explainer: Each modality needs its own gold data: scanned forms, charts, accents, noisy audio. Test adversarial images, including text hidden in pixels that tries to inject instructions. Scan uploaded files for malware before processing. Accessibility matters too: generated alt text and transcripts should be checked for accuracy, since users may rely on them. Try it: build 20 test images that contain hidden text instructions, and check whether your pipeline obeys any of them.

quiz.q: Prefer text extraction before VLM when…
choices: Digital text PDFs are available and reliable
Every input is a photo of a whiteboard
quiz.why: Cheaper and often more accurate.

quiz.q: A cost-aware document pipeline usually starts with…
choices: Sending every page as an image
Text extraction and OCR, with VLM fallback
quiz.why: Text paths are cheaper and often more accurate.

quiz.q: "Prompt injection in pixels" refers to…
choices: Instructions hidden in images that a VLM may follow
quiz.why: Vision inputs are another untrusted channel.

lesson.intuition: Accepting images, PDFs and audio changes your app's contract. Files can be huge, malicious, low quality or full of hidden instructions, and each modality needs its own processing and evaluation. Good multimodal products put gates and pipelines in the API, use the cheapest path that works (often text extraction) and test on the messy inputs real users send.
how: Gate uploads: size limits, MIME allowlists, malware scanning.
Route by modality: text extraction or OCR first for documents, VLM fallback for complex layouts, STT for audio, screenshot understanding for UIs.
Treat all extracted content as untrusted input (it can contain prompt injection).
Build modality-specific eval sets, including photos of pages, noisy audio and adversarial images.
Design accessible outputs, such as alt text and transcripts.
lesson.example: Choosing the cheaper path: a 20-page digital PDF has extractable text of about 10,000 tokens. Sending it as 20 page images to a VLM might cost roughly 1,500 image tokens per page, 30,000 tokens. Text extraction first is about 3× cheaper and only pages with figures need the VLM.
mistakes: No upload size limit or file-type allowlist.
Evaluating only on clean digital PDFs when users send phone photos.
Letting text inside images change the agent's instructions or permissions.
lesson.enterprise: An insurance claims app accepts photos, PDFs and voice notes. Uploads are scanned and size-limited, voice notes are transcribed, PDFs use text extraction with a VLM fallback for damage photos, and adjusters see transcripts and extracted fields side by side.
takeaways: Gate files in the API, not the prompt.
Cheapest modality path first.
Eval on messy real inputs.

subjects.title: RL Environments, Reward Design and Prompt Optimization
subjects.why: Post-training for agents is now mostly environment and reward engineering; the quality of the environment decides what the model learns.
subjects.explainer:
Reinforcement learning for LLM agents needs three things: an environment (tasks plus sandboxed tools such as code execution, a browser or a simulated company), a reward (verifiable checks like tests passing or a correct database state, or graders and reward models), and an RL algorithm (PPO, GRPO and variants) run by a framework such as verl, OpenRLHF or TRL with fast rollouts on vLLM.

Environment design is the hard part: tasks must be diverse, realistic, solvable and verifiable, at the right difficulty for the current model. Reward hacking is the central failure: the policy finds ways to score without solving the task, such as editing tests, special-casing graders or exploiting simulator bugs. Defenses include hidden tests, multiple independent graders, monitoring trajectories and held-out evals.

Before spending GPUs on RL, prompt and program optimization can capture much of the gain: DSPy compiles prompts and few-shot examples against a metric, and GEPA evolves prompts using reflective feedback on trajectories. Model merging (for example with mergekit) combines fine-tuned checkpoints without further training.

Common mistakes: rewards that can be gamed; environments far easier than production; no held-out evaluation; training on contaminated benchmark data.

Mental model: the model optimizes exactly what you reward, in the world you built for it.

topics.title: Environments and verifiable rewards
topics.explainer: An RL environment for agents exposes a task, tools and a final check. Verifiable rewards come from deterministic checks: unit tests, exact answers, database end states, or a compiler. Gym-style interfaces (reset, step, reward) make environments reusable. Sandboxed execution in containers keeps rollouts safe and reproducible at scale. Tune difficulty so the model succeeds sometimes; tasks that are always solved or never solved give no learning signal under group-relative methods like GRPO.

subtopics.title: Gym-style reset/step/reward
subtopics.text: A reset/step/reward API (from OpenAI Gym, now Gymnasium) makes environments interchangeable across RL frameworks.

subtopics.title: Difficulty calibration
subtopics.text: Keep tasks the model sometimes solves; always-solved and never-solved tasks give no learning signal.

topics.title: Reward hacking and environment quality
topics.explainer: Reward hacking happens when the policy maximizes the reward signal without achieving the intended goal, for example deleting failing tests, hard-coding expected outputs or exploiting a lenient judge. Detect it by sampling and reading trajectories, comparing reward with held-out evaluation, and watching for sudden reward jumps. Prevent it with hidden or regenerated tests, read-only graders, multiple reward sources, penalties for forbidden actions, and environment red-teaming before training starts.

subtopics.title: Common reward hacks
subtopics.text: Common hacks include editing tests, hard-coding expected outputs and exploiting grader bugs.

subtopics.title: Hidden tests and read-only graders
subtopics.text: Keep tests hidden from the policy and graders read-only so they can't be modified during rollouts.

topics.title: Prompt optimization, RL frameworks and merging
topics.explainer: Prompt and program optimizers search over instructions and examples against your metric: DSPy compiles modular programs; GEPA uses reflection on failed trajectories to evolve prompts and often rivals RL at a fraction of the cost. When weights must change, frameworks such as verl, OpenRLHF and TRL orchestrate rollouts, reward computation and PPO or GRPO updates. Model merging averages or combines fine-tuned weights to blend skills cheaply; always re-evaluate merged models.

subtopics.title: DSPy optimizers
subtopics.text: DSPy optimizers tune prompts and few-shot examples automatically against a metric, with no weight updates.

subtopics.title: Model merging with mergekit
subtopics.text: Mergekit combines the weights of fine-tuned models of the same architecture to blend their skills.

quiz.q: Why are tasks the model always solves useless for GRPO?
choices: All samples get the same reward, so group-relative advantages are zero
quiz.why: GRPO learns from reward differences within a group; identical rewards give no signal.

quiz.q: Training reward rises sharply but held-out success is flat. Most likely?
quiz.why: Divergence between reward and held-out evals signals the policy is gaming the reward.

quiz.q: What should you try before spending GPUs on RL?
choices: Prompt/program optimization (DSPy, GEPA) against the same metric
quiz.why: Prompt optimization often captures much of the gain cheaply.

lesson.intuition: Reinforcement learning for agents is like building a flight simulator and a scoring system for a trainee pilot. The simulator (environment) gives realistic tasks and tools; the score (reward) says whether the task was really done. The model practices many times and learns what scores well, so if the simulator or score is flawed, it learns the flaw.
how: Build an environment with a Gym-style interface: reset gives a task, step runs an action, and the environment returns observations and rewards.
Use verifiable rewards where possible: tests passing, correct database state, exact answers; use graders or reward models otherwise.
Run many sandboxed rollouts in parallel with fast inference (for example vLLM inside frameworks like verl, OpenRLHF or TRL).
Audit trajectories for reward hacking and compare reward with held-out evals.
Consider cheaper alternatives first: prompt optimization (DSPy, GEPA) or model merging.
lesson.example: Difficulty calibration: if a task's pass rate is 0% or 100% across all samples, GRPO-style group advantages are zero and the task teaches nothing. With 8 samples per task, a pass rate around 25-75% gives the most signal. Of 5,000 candidate tasks, a team keeps the 2,300 whose initial pass rate falls between 10% and 90%.
mistakes: Rewards the model can satisfy without doing the task, such as editable tests or checks that only look at output format.
Tasks that are all too easy or too hard, giving no learning signal.
Trusting rising reward without checking held-out evals.
lesson.enterprise: A company building a spreadsheet agent creates 3,000 tasks with target workbook states as rewards, in sandboxes with read-only graders. Weekly trajectory audits caught the agent deleting rows to make a sum check pass; the grader now checks the full table.
takeaways: The environment and reward define what is learned.
Prefer verifiable, hard-to-game rewards.
Audit trajectories; watch held-out evals.

subjects.title: Image and Video Generation: Diffusion Models in Products
subjects.why: Generative media is part of many agent workflows (marketing, design, product content), and it brings its own cost, safety and IP questions.
subjects.explainer:
Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a noising process: starting from random noise, a network repeatedly predicts and removes noise, guided by a text prompt. Latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion) runs this in a compressed latent space for speed; diffusion transformers (DiT) replaced the U-Net backbone in many recent models; flow matching is a closely related training objective. Video models extend this across time. Control methods (ControlNet, image-to-image, inpainting) and fine-tuning (LoRA, DreamBooth) shape outputs to a brand or subject.

In agentic products, an agent might write a brief, call an image or video generation API, check the output with a vision model, and iterate. Production concerns: cost per image or second of video, latency, content safety filters, provenance marking (C2PA, and EU AI Act Article 50 duties to mark synthetic content), likeness and IP rights, and human review for public assets.

Common mistakes: no safety filter on prompts and outputs; no record of model and prompt for provenance; ignoring licensing of training data and outputs.

Mental model: generation is cheap to try and expensive to trust; build the review loop first.

topics.title: How diffusion models work
topics.explainer: Training adds Gaussian noise to images over many steps and teaches a network to predict that noise given the noisy image, the step and a text embedding. Generation starts from pure noise and denoises step by step. Latent diffusion compresses images with an autoencoder so denoising runs on small latents. Classifier-free guidance strengthens prompt adherence by mixing conditional and unconditional predictions. Fewer sampling steps via better samplers or distillation cut latency at some quality cost.

subtopics.title: Forward noising and reverse denoising
subtopics.text: The forward process adds Gaussian noise over many steps; the model learns to reverse each step by predicting the added noise.

subtopics.title: Classifier-free guidance
subtopics.text: Classifier-free guidance blends predictions with and without the prompt; higher guidance follows the prompt more closely but can reduce variety.

subtopics.title: Samplers and step distillation
subtopics.text: Samplers decide how to step from noise to image; distilled models can produce good images in just a few steps.

topics.title: Control, customization and video
topics.explainer: Image-to-image, inpainting and outpainting edit existing images. ControlNet and similar adapters condition on edges, poses or depth for layout control. LoRA and DreamBooth fine-tune a model on a few images of a product, style or person. Video diffusion models add temporal layers or operate on spatio-temporal latents, with cost scaling with resolution and duration. Agents can orchestrate these steps, but each one needs automated checks.

subtopics.title: Inpainting and outpainting
subtopics.text: Inpainting regenerates a masked region of an image; outpainting extends it beyond its borders.

subtopics.title: ControlNet conditioning
subtopics.text: ControlNet adds a conditioning input, such as a pose, edge map or depth map, to control composition.

subtopics.title: LoRA and DreamBooth customization
subtopics.text: LoRA and DreamBooth adapt an image model to a specific subject or style with a few example images.

topics.title: Safety, provenance and cost in production
topics.explainer: Filter prompts and outputs for disallowed content, and block likeness of real people without consent. Mark outputs as AI-generated with C2PA manifests or watermarks, which supports EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations for synthetic content. Log the model, prompt, seed and reviewer for each published asset. Track cost per approved asset, not per generation, since rejected attempts add up. Clarify licensing and IP terms of the model and outputs before commercial use.

subtopics.title: Likeness and consent
subtopics.text: Generating a real person's likeness or voice needs their consent and clear policy.

subtopics.title: C2PA provenance and watermarking
subtopics.text: C2PA content credentials attach signed metadata describing how an asset was made; watermarks embed signals in the pixels.

subtopics.title: Cost per approved asset
subtopics.text: Divide total generation cost by the number of assets actually approved, since many drafts are discarded.

quiz.q: What does a diffusion model learn during training?
choices: To predict the noise added to an image at a given step
quiz.why: It learns to denoise; generation runs that in reverse from noise.

quiz.q: Why does latent diffusion run faster?
choices: Denoising happens in a compressed latent space
quiz.why: Smaller latents make each denoising step cheaper.

quiz.q: Which practice supports transparency duties for synthetic images?
quiz.why: Provenance marking identifies content as AI-generated.

lesson.intuition: Image and video generators start from pure noise and clean it up step by step until a picture matching the prompt appears, like a sculptor removing marble. In products they power marketing images, design variations and video drafts, and they bring their own costs, safety checks, likeness and copyright questions, and the need to label AI-made content.
how: Training: add noise to real images in many steps (forward process) and train a network to predict the noise (reverse process).
Latent diffusion runs this in a compressed latent space from an autoencoder, which is much cheaper than pixels.
Generation: start from noise and denoise in a number of sampler steps, guided by the text prompt (classifier-free guidance).
Control outputs with image-to-image, inpainting, ControlNet conditioning or LoRA fine-tunes for a brand or product.
In production: safety filters, consent for likenesses, provenance (C2PA) and cost tracking per approved asset.
lesson.example: Cost per approved asset: generating an image costs $0.04 and a reviewer approves 1 in 5, so model cost per approved image is $0.20. Adding review time of 30 seconds per candidate at $40 per hour (≈ $0.33 per candidate) makes the true cost ≈ 5 × ($0.04 + $0.33) ≈ $1.87 per approved image. Better prompts or a LoRA that lift approval to 1 in 2 cut that to ≈ $0.75.
mistakes: Counting only generation cost and ignoring human review time.
Generating images of real people without consent.
Publishing AI-generated media with no provenance or disclosure where it is required or expected.
lesson.enterprise: A retailer generates lifestyle images of its products with a LoRA trained on approved product photos. Every image carries C2PA content credentials, passes a safety filter, and is logged with prompt and model version for audit.
takeaways: Diffusion = learned denoising from noise to image.
Control methods make outputs on-brand.
Measure cost per approved asset; add provenance.
